That this House condemns the Government for its inadequate response to the growing financial crisis in the agriculture sector and for its failure to provide sufficient support and services to farmers who face severe economic difficulties in all regions of the country.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion which you have just read to the House underlines a very acute problem for our farmers right across Canada. Of the 300,000 farms in Canada, thousands are in deep trouble. This is an industry which should claim the attention of the House. There is over $187 billion in growth production in agriculture and those industries related to agriculture in Canada. One in six jobs in this country is related to agriculture. It is the most important sector in the country.
We not only have the duty to boost our economy by farm production, but I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you will not reject the proposition that we have the potential in Canada to feed a hungry world. We have the duty to ensure that our agricultural production is mustered and marshalled so that we feed our neighbours throughout the globe who are starving.
This is the most productive industry in the country. Eugene Whelan, who was a great Minister of Agriculture for 12 years, never failed to remind Canadians, when addressing either an urban or rural audience, that when it came to productivity and efficiency the farmers in Canada were the most efficient in the world and the farming industry in Canada was the most efficient in the country.
I bring the motion to the attention of the House and Canadians because, despite that potential, farmers today face all kinds of uncertainties. Not only do they face the traditional unpredictable weather but in parts of western Canada they
face floods, drought and an economic climate which is uncertain. Farmers have struggled through three or four years of inflation and recession, price fluctuation and uncertainty of markets.
The farming community in this country includes the best of our entrepreneurs, the best of the free market spirit. They are the real risk takers in Canada. They need our support and encouragement. Most of all, the farmers of Canada want their Governments, federal and provincial, to treat them fairly. They do not want handouts or something for nothing. They want fairness.
The purpose of this debate is to draw to the attention of the House and the country the fact that the Government is not keeping its solemn commitment to treat the farmers in this country with fairness or understanding. Instead, since coming into office the Government has undertaken almost a systematic campaign to renege on those promises it made during the election campaign.
Farming is important in every province of the country but I would say particularly in western Canada. As I travelled in western Canada since the election, the question I heard throughout the West was why the Government, with its overwhelming majority of Members from western Canada, has been treating farmers in such a callous and off-handed matter.

speechtext:
The motion which is before the House today was introduced by the Official Opposition. It condemns the Government for its inadequate response to the growing financial crisis in agriculture, and also points to the failure of the Government in not providing sufficient support and services to farmers who are facing severe economic crises.
The economic statement of November 8 indicated the direction which this Government was taking. I believe farmers received the very clear message from that statement that agriculture would not be as high a priority after the election as it was before the election. We only have to look at the various cut-backs which were proposed in that statement to realize that. Cut-backs in the Department of Agriculture amounted to $62.9 million.
Some of those cut-backs were very hard to rationalize, if we view them in straight business terms. For instance, the cutbacks in Canagrex which the Government says will mean a savings next year of $6.6 million, my information is that so far this year about $3 million has been spent. With two months yet to go, spending will not be anything approaching the $6.6 million. Information the Government has provided indicates that there was between $16 million and $17 million worth of sales completed in the first five months of operation, with something over $100 million in progress. That seems to me to be a cost-benefit ratio of about 2 per cent to 3 per cent of sales.
It may not be widely known, but farmers see overseas sales as new business, which I think is the case with anyone who has ever been in business, and they see this agency as providing them with something in the neighbourhood of $100 million worth of business which would not otherwise have occurred, all at a cost to the treasury of $2 million to $3 million thus far. I think most business people would think that was a pretty good return on investment.
However, the Government, for its own reasons, chose to abandon that particular agency. I think this had nothing to do with dollars and cents, Mr. Speaker, or providing a needed service to farmers. However, it had everything to do with the Government's own philosophy regarding Crown corporations and the Tories' long and arduous struggle to oppose Canagrex when they were in opposition. I think the Government would be well advised to admit that it is for philosophical rather than business reasons that Canagrex is being shut down.
Additional attempts to reduce Department of Agriculture expenditures are also aimed at exports to some degree. The Government is proposing to reduce assistance to the Canadian Dairy Commission in its efforts to increase exports of cheese and dairy products. The reduction is some $4 million in the coming year and will increase to a full $6.6 million in the year following.
I think the more noticeable form of cuts lies in the fees the Government is now proposing to charge for inspections done on behalf of Canadians and therefore normally paid on their behalf by the Government. It is now proposing to collect these fees from the agricultural producers and processors. Some $32
million is projected to be collected. The Government is attempting to collect a fee for meat inspection, as well as replacing some federal inspection with in-plant inspection. All of this has raised a great deal of concern among consumers as well as people in the industry.
The question arises as to whom the inspectors will be acting for. If the plant pays for the inspection service and hires the inspector, will the consumer be adequately protected? Further questions have arisen regarding the inspection of imported meat. I am sure the House will recall the recent report from Halifax where the federal inspector decided there was too much hair and manure in a shipment of imported meat. On appeal to the Department of Agriculture veterinarian, the meat was permitted to enter. This sort of thing has happened on several different occasions. The argument is not over whether the veterinarian or the meat inspector has jurisdiction; it is over the attempt to switch responsibility from a federal agency to an importer or processor.
Another concern arises from the very rapid increase in fees which producers have been paying. I will cite only one example in the time I have. Seedgrowers in this country have just found out that an Order in Council has been prepared which indicates they will pay fees from 400 per cent to 500 per cent higher than they were last year. The Government is pretending to have consultation with the people concerned but the negotiating room the seedgrowers have is very limited when the Order in Council is ready to go.
Another area of cut-backs which does not seem to make any sense on the surface, and I hope eventually the Government will provide a better explanation than it has to this point, deals with the decision to cease the inquiry into potato marketing in the five eastern provinces. As the House may be aware, that particular industry has been studied for the last 13 or 14 years. All these studies have resulted in some dissatisfaction among all parties concerned because it was always felt the real truth had not been sorted out. A decision was taken some time ago to set up the judicial inquiry with a judge at the helm who would have the power to subpoena witnesses and their records so that the real truth could be found. However, apparently someone on the Government's side felt this might be threatening to some of their particular friends and that investigation ceased forthwith.
Farmers are still asking questions about the marketing of potatoes and are quite unhappy the real truth was not dug into. I think the new Government had a very clear and fresh mandate and certainly looking into the true facts of potato marketing would have been a suitable beginning for a new Government. I am sorry the Tories saw fit to stop this one chance to shed a little light on some of the inner workings of the Canadian potato marketing system.
The Government announced during its economic statement in November that it would be discussing three taxation issues affecting farmers. There were very clear promises in the election campaign to do away with capital gains taxes. In some of the back roads of the country it was simply referred to as doing away with capital gains. Perhaps those people were more
February 5, 1985

right than they know when you look at the price of farm land, which is going down in virtually all parts of the country. Perhaps it is part of the Government's economic policy to run agriculture into the ground so that the capital gains in farm land which accrued with inflation will now reverse itself and we will go back to 1971 prices. Of course, the Government will then indeed have done away with capital gains. However, I think it was the taxes that they were promising to do away with.
As well the Tories promised to make some drastic changes to Section 31 of the Income Tax Act and implement something called an agri-bond, although their particular description was never made very clear. In the few places where it was described it sounded somewhat like the agri-bond which is in place in the United States that provides a tax break for investors. It has proven to be a rather inefficient way of providing assistance to farmers since the forgone income revenue from the Government amounts to several times what the direct cost would have been had they simply subsidized the farmer who is eligible to receive the borrowed back money which has been invested in agri-bonds.
On November 7 we were promised that there would be an interparliamentary committee set up to study these issues. To my knowledge, the committee has not yet been named. However, we do have a discussion paper which came out last Thursday or Friday. Some of the issues that the Government is proposing to put forward for discussion are focused on the wrong areas. For instance, it is fairly clear from the discussion paper that with regard to in-family roll-overs, relatively wealthy farms have no problem with capital gains tax. They generate enough funds to enable the existing generation of farmers to provide themselves with savings and retirement funds, meanwhile rolling the farm over to their sons, daughters or grandchildren. However, the middle and lower income farmers do not usually have that kind of income. Therefore, the roll-over provision is not so helpful to them. They are forced to sell all or part of the farm and to pay some capital gains tax. The current system is working quite well for the relatively wealthy but not so well for the middle and lower income people.
The treatment of farm losses by Revenue Canada was a real eye opener. I could conceptually understand that high income people would get the biggest benefit. However, the discussion paper includes some studies which show just how much benefit high income people receive by writing losses off against a farm. Table 13 of that discussion paper indicates that the average off-farm income of 105 returns was $406,000. Their farms were relatively large, having an average gross farm sales of $120,000. The surprising thing is that our tax system permits a relatively large farm with gross sales of $120,000 to have an average farm loss of $187,000. A person with off-farm income of $406,000 pays tax on $219,000.
There are about 1,700 taxpayers who have off-farm earnings in excess of $100,000. Virtually all of those in that category
Supply
write off about 50 per cent more than the farm actually generates in total sales. I am referring to total sales rather than profits, Mr. Speaker. Anyone who knows farming knows that the money left over for wages and reinvestment tends to be in the range of 14 per cent to 20 per cent. Yet the focus of Section 31 seems to be on people whose off-farm incomes run from $10,000 to $25,000. Ironically, these people run farms with gross sales which far exceed the amount of losses that are written off against them. These are almost economical units in terms of cash flow in and losses out. Yet those are the people whom we have been concentrating on. There do not seem to be any proposals in the discussion paper to change the focus or to concentrate on the real tax outflows.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that in the first four or five months that the Government has been in power it has given some very clear indications of what it thinks of agriculture. It has made some promises which it has yet to keep concerning the establishment of an inter-parliamentary committee to study the three issues I have just been talking about; capital gains tax, Section 31, and agri-bonds. The Government is acting on its serious intention to cut some $63 million from the agriculture budget. We have only begun to see how this will cost in terms of extra fees for service. We have only begun to see, as the seed growers have found out, that it can be very expensive to become self-sufficient in the area of supply and services for farmers.
The current Government seems to have no real understanding of the need for expansion of trade in agriculture. By cutting back on the dairy program and doing away with Canagrex it has thrown out the baby with the bath water. The Government has washed its hands of in excess of $100 million of new business. We will remember that two years from now when we assess the Government's commitment to agriculture. It will be measured by how it replaced those programs and how much money was spent on their replacement. We will be watching these things because the moves the Government has made so far do not make very much economic sense.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the agriculture critic for the New Democratic Party. There is a small number of farmers in my riding. One of the complaints I have been receiving from them over the last number of years concerns the effect of interest rates especially on young farmers and those farming in frontier regions such as exist in my riding. Equipment is expensive and farmers are trying to develop agricultural lands, which means that returns are limited at the beginning.
Today's paper indicated that the Canadian dollar is again threatened. In the last five years, every time the Canadian dollar was threatened with devaluation, the Liberal Government and the preceding Conservative Government jacked up interest rates. In the Member's opinion, what would be the effect of another period of high interest rates in Canada?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-SUPPORT FOR AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suggest the answer is quite clear to everyone in the House. Farmers are losing their farms as a result of a number of years in which interest rates were extremely high compared to the money being earned. That combined with permission to grant loans that float instead of being set for fixed terms at fixed rates created havoc for farmers and small businessmen as well as home owners.
A resumption of an increase in interest rates will only make banks and credit organizations much more nervous and will probably result in more foreclosures of farms, particularly before the spring seeding season begins.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to address the subject of the Opposition motion that was introduced by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). I must repeat what I said in the period following the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition's remarks. It is the fact that he did not provide us with an answer to why he decided to replace Eugene Whelan as Minister of Agriculture. He did not use the opportunity to explain to the House and the agricultural community in particular why, during his term of office, he did not move at all to provide interest rate subsidies to FCC clients who were locked into high interest rates. Indeed, it appeared that during his term of office interest rates for FCC clients were quite satisfactory at a rate of 16.75 per cent.
I would also like to clarify for the record that the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition confused the Prince Albert statement with a letter which was written to the President of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture on July 17 of last year and signed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). The
Leader of the Opposition was extremely selective in assessing what action had been taken on those 11 points which we put to the President of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture on July 17. In order to set the record straight, it would be interesting to see exactly what the Ontario Federation of Agriculture has indicated with respect to those commitments made by the Prime Minister on July 17.
A brief was submitted to all Members of Parliament on January 31 of this year. It contains a report, or assessment perhaps, which was made by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, a very respectable farm organization in Ontario. In the opinion of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, action has been taken with regard to our commitment on agri-bonds. That has been referred to a parliamentary committee.
The OFA has indicated that action has been taken with respect to the second commitment about Section 31. That has been referred to a parliamentary committee.
Our third commitment refers to capital gains. It should be noted that farm organizations have been making representations to the federal Government on these three items for many years. In fact, the Liberal Government has been in office for most of that period in the last 10 to 15 years. That Government chose to ignore these three items.
The fourth commitment was to take action on the advance payments legislation. Indeed, legislation is presently being drafted and will be introduced in the House very soon.
With respect to the fifth commitment on stabilization, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition should know that that Bill has been introduced in the House of Commons. I expect that it will be debated very soon and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
Item No. 7 dealt with the commitment to the Farm Credit Corporation. Indeed, the Ontario Federation of Agriculture assessed this item as action being taken. All members have copies of this brief that was presented on January 31 of this year. I would draw the attention of Members to the letter to all Members of Parliament that was signed by the President of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture. The second to last paragraph states:
The OFA was heartened by the announcements of Agriculture Minister John Wise regarding assistance to farm operations in financial difficulty.
I believe the statements made by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture certainly justify its position with reference to action we have taken.
There is more. In the opinion of the OFA action has been taken on the commitment to set up farm finance review boards. Indeed, the right Hon. gentleman recognized that we have established Farm Credit Appeal Boards in this country to deal with cases of severe financial distress. In addition, there is the pilot project taking place in the counties of Bruce and Grey in Ontario.
Commitment No. 9 was to take action on beef imports into this country. The Canadian beef industry made constant representations to the Liberals when they were in office. Yet when the Liberals were in office and the leader of the Opposi-
February 5, 1985

tion was Prime Minister, he chose once again to turn his back on the agriculture community. He took no action whatsoever and, as a result, the Canadian beef industry suffered losses of between $25 million and $50 million.
We did not ignore the Canadian agriculture industry or the Canadian beef industry. Indeed, in co-operation with my caucus colleagues and Cabinet colleagues, we invoked the beef import law.
With respect to Item No. 11, it was another commitment given at Prince Albert in which we indicated that the food producers of this country would receive a tax rebate to offset the additional energy costs. Although it is a budgetary item and it would have been appropriate to provide that rebate, we did not wait for a budget to implement that. Parliament opened on a Monday and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) gave a statement on the Thursday and provided that benefit to Canadian food producers. That will provide a benefit to Canadian food producers to the extent of $100 million. That is the further commitment we gave for the promise that we made and the further actions that we have taken and fulfilled.
It goes on, Mr. Speaker. We are up to item No. 12. These items raised back in July totalled 11, but we are now up to 12 items. This was a commitment we gave during the campaign to amend the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act to allow tobacco growers, if they so choose, to establish a national marketing agency. We did not turn our backs on the tobacco producers of this country at all. We gave them a commitment in June. The election was held. Canadian agriculture turned its back on the Liberal Party. It supported us and we accepted our obligations and responsibilities. We provided the required amendment in the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act. Hearings are now going forward and it is up to the tobacco growers to determine whether they will establish a national marketing agency.
In addition to that, an issue that has always been an issue on which I have been fighting for a good long time is the decision of the Liberal Government to cancel the offshore labour program. The Liberals did not recognize the need for that program, particularly in southwestern Ontario and in other parts of the country where we have large orchard operations in fruit and vegetables, tobacco, et cetera.
It is absolutely essential that we have that offshore labour program. I can remember when I first arrived here in 1972. The Government at that time was, of course, a Liberal Government. It made up its mind, as it did it almost each and every year without exception, and was determined to wind that program down. If that were ever allowed to happen it would create very serious economic consequences to agriculture in many parts of the country. If it had not been for the Hon. Member for Haldimand-Norfolk (Mr. Bradley), the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday), the Hon. Member for Kent, at the time and myself, I am certain that the Liberal Government would have succeeded.

We did not hold the industry out this year at all. We met with the commodity organizations and the groups that were extremely interested in having the offshore labour program announced and announced early. My colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), a few weeks ago took an early opportunity to signal to that particular segment in the agri-food industry that the offshore labour program would continue for this crop year.
We also made it clear that the European student program would be in place. As well, the clarification with reference to the metric policy was made in a statement the other day to the House by my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote). That measure caused chaos and confusion, has resulted in a number of court cases and unfortunately a number of crop losses due to the problem of trying to convert from one system to another or to one system only. Perhaps an imperial sprayer or something of that nature was involved. The Liberals always ignored that problem. They did not understand some of the difficulties that program caused in the field and at the farm level. That move on behalf of this Government will bring an end to chaos and confusion and add some common sense and clarity to the situation.
In conjunction with my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty), we have responded to representations by caucus colleagues, particularly the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), with reference to some changes in the national revenue policy of this Government. This will allow farmers who have received cash payments of one kind or the other the opportunity to work out an agreement with National Revenue to roll those receipts into next year. That is helpful.

Some of the things that I have mentioned at the end are not of large national significance, but I mention them because I think it is movements and measures of these kinds which signal to the farm community that we understand some of their individual and smaller problems. It is a message that we want to send to them. We do not have much money. We are committed to lowering the deficit and we should never lose sight of that. If we do, then we will fall into that route to disaster, the road to bankruptcy, followed by the previous Government. That means total and complete disaster for the agricultural industry.
The state of the agricultural industry is determined to a large extent by the state of the general economy. Perhaps this industry more than any other industry in Canada is affected in that way. An industry that might compare would be the small business community. But other than that one exception, the economic well-being and health of the agriculture industry is determined by the state of the general economy. There is no question about that. We can provide bits of stabilization here and there. We have and we will continue to do so. But let us not be distracted by thinking that by moving a little here and moving a little there it will resolve this economic problem we have, because obviously it will not.

I talk to people in the industry. The Right Eton. Leader of the Opposition indicated that I should travel across Canada more. I should love to do that. I think I have made three or four trips to western Canada. I have made two or three trips to eastern Canada and I have been in the Province of Quebec on three or four occasions. Leader of the Opposition, I would not be here today; I would be in the Province of Quebec, I would be involved in a sod-turning ceremony at a research facility in St. Hyacinthe, a $17 million project. We in this party have our priorities set properly. I am interested and all of our caucus and Cabinet colleagues in this Government are interested in dealing with the farm finance problem. It is our number one problem and we are making it our number one concern. It was not a hard decision for me to make to cancel these plans that have been in place for quite some time. I made a decision that indeed this was the place to be. It is not often that we have the agricultural issue raised by the Official Opposition.
I think the spokesmen for the New Democratic Party recognized the importance of this issue. I am not sure how much time I have remaining. I have not as yet referred to any of my notes because I felt that we had a tendency to be somewhat misled by some of the comments made by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition. However, there is no question: the record is clear and speaks for itself. The Liberals completely ignored the agricultural community for years and years and years; there is no question about that. The same farm organizations have been making representations to government year after year. We know them by their first names from coast to coast. We almost recognize their voices when we talk to them on the telephone. However, the fact of the matter is that the Liberal Party was in government for years and years and it ignored these problems. It paid lip service to the agri-food industry. We are not doing that. We have not been in office that long, but I challenge any statements by the Official Opposition. It has challenged our actions in a hundred days in terms of what we have provided to the agricultural industry. We are not satisfied. We have only just
begun. I would compare any of our hundred days with any of their hundred days.

I was surprised that the Minister did not spend more time talking about the farm financial crisis. Not one research facility has been cancelled within Agriculture Canada. Two projects came on stream from found money. They involved two laboratories, one at Three Rivers and one at Victoriaville. speechtext:
I am just saying how sorry we are that the Minister cannot be in St. Hyacinthe today for that official opening. Being such a great House of Commons man, I know in his heart he would really rather be here today.
This Government seems to be caught up in the process and the optics of government-not really taking action but seeming to perform. We saw the symbolic signing of a cheque by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle). With great flourish he signed a $13 million cheque for the pork producers. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and this Government love that kind of symbolism. They love to be seen to be doing something. Studying agri-bonds, Section 31 and the problems of agriculture is just as good to them as taking action. From a superficial point of view, they may appear to be actually doing something. However, when you get down to the individual pork producers in the Province of Quebec, they will call the Minister of Public Works to account for that cheque. They are going to go to the bank and try to cash that cheque. Regardless of how much the Minister of Agriculture pooh-poohs the action, the pork producers in the Province of Quebec will not be put off.
In this whole process, the Government is abandoning many of our agricultural producers. The Farm Credit Corporation report showed that 39,000 farmers are in serious financial difficulties. This morning the Minister spoke and responded for 10 minutes. He did not say how he was going to help the
39,000	farmers in very serious difficulty. These are real people. It is not the agricultural producers who are the best off. If they spend more than 40 per cent of their cash flow to pay debts, if their quota is less than 15 per cent of their operation or if they are borrowing more than what they are spending on capital expenditures, their finances are in a very serious position. The tragedy is that they are the young farmers, those who have been in agriculture for 11 years on average.
Beyond that, those farmers are really our hope for the future because they are the most productive and technically advanced farmers and produce half of all the food produced in this country. It is just not factual for the Government to say that
by reducing interest rates from 14 per cent to 12.75 per cent, we will solve all the problems. I do not know how to describe that other than by saying it is just not factual.
Last week I saw a farmer in my office who was with the OFA group. He described how he bought his hog-producing farm for $320,000 ten years ago. He took out a $240,000 mortgage with the FCC. He had the farm appraised last summer because he had heard some stories about farm properties dropping in value. In fact, his appraisal came out to $165,000. He has lost half his equity in the last two or three years. I would like to know how the Minister's little reduction in interest rates from 14 per cent to 12.75 per cent will help that producer.
The 70,000 or 75,000 agricultural producers in the country carry $17 billion worth of the $21 billion over-all debt in this country today. When the Farm Credit Corporation appeared before the Agriculture Committee, it indicated that in the next year or two there will be defaults of about $2 billion on these farm loans. That is a colossal amount of money. I do not know how many thousands of farmers it represents. It would seem to be very, very many of them. In fact, Ralph Ashmead, a research analyst for the Farm Credit Corporation, said in an interview recorded in The Manitoba Co-operator back in October that he estimated that there were between 2,000 and
3,000	farmers who were headed for immediate financial collapse.
I was surprised that the Minister spoke of the lack of success of the American farm set-aside program. That program is designed to help the farmers whose equity has dropped dramatically like the farmer from Nipissing to whom I referred. Obviously it is a program which will not help all farmers. If a farmer has lost his equity, no program can help him. However, when setting aside a portion of the debt for a number of years will put the farmer in a positive cash flow position and give him a margin of approximately 10 per cent, then the American Farmers Home Administration which is similar to our Farm Credit Corporation will set aside that debt and pay the interest on one-quarter of the debt for up to five years.
The Minister of Agriculture has no program of a similar calibre. One could say: "That is really only bailing someone out. Should we actually do that?" I say that we should consider very seriously doing that in this country. Every time the Farm Credit Corporation has a default, a bankruptcy or a foreclosure, it loses between $80,000 and $90,000. We know that when there is a bankruptcy, half of the stock is replaced and half of the chattels walk away overnight. Rather than losing $80,000 or $90,000 in a foreclosure, why not assist a farmer by setting aside a portion of his debt, thereby putting him in a positive cash flow position for several years and ultimately allowing him to be responsible for his debt at a later time?
In September when the farm debt crisis began in the United States and farm property values dropped by 25 per cent to 50 per cent there and in Canada, the Americans announced this set-aside program and the Farmers Home Administration sent

out notices of it to about 150,000 of its clients. As well, it has received over 100,000 inquiries from people asking about the program and whether or not they can take advantage of it. 3,000	farm set-asides.

We are disappointed that the Government has decided to cancel Canagrex. When the Tories were campaigning in the last election they talked about Canada becoming a superpower in agricultural exports. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has now been two months since the report by Judge Rosalie Abella was tabled, and the Progressive Conservative Party has yet to respond to the 117 recommendations for dealing with problems related to job discrimination.
This is a matter that requires special attention and immediate action, especially /Where visible minorities are concerned, as demonstrated in a joint study prepared by the Toronto Metro Social Planning Council and the Urban Alliance on Race Relations. Mr. Speaker, last week the P.E.I. Potato Marketing Board and the P.E.I. Potato Producers' Association received letters from the Deputy Minister of Agriculture outlining increases in potato inspection and certification fees, considered as cost recovery measures by the Department of Agriculture.
Inspection fees for table stock potatoes are to be 33 cents per hundredweight, effective April 1 this year. When we look at the average yield based on Prince Edward Island production of 200 hundredweight per acre, that means the cost per acre will jump to $66. For the average farmer who produces 200 acres of potatoes, that means over $13,000 in inspection fees.
A fee has also been introduced for seed potato producers which, on average, would amount to about $5,000 in most cases. This will be prohibitive to many farmers who are already finding it difficult to get their products to market at a price above the cost of production.
The potato producers of Prince Edward Island are opposed to this new fee structure. They are particularly concerned that the changes will come into effect without consultation, and apparently without compromise. TREATMENT OF DETAINEES CLAIMING REFUGEE STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, refugees and other persons who arrive by aeroplane at Pearson International Airport and are for any reason detained at the minimum security facility in the Avion Motor Hotel, ought to be treated no worse than criminals condemned to imprisonment in Canada. However, I am advised that indeed they are. I have been told that they never receive as much as one full hour per day outside in the fresh air. In fact, more often than not they receive none.
Detainees are strictly forbidden to talk with each other, even in the line-up for meals. There is no library. Security staff arbitrarily search the detainees' rooms and stored belongings, without permission, and some detainees allege their belongings have been stolen. The security staff frequently use abusive language and, ironically, threaten detainees with jail.
1 call upon the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) to inquire into the operation of this detention facility and report to this House on whether Canada
meets the expectations of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees, and in particular, as to who determines the rules governing detainees, who is responsible for administering them, and what recourse is open to a detainee who feels unjustly treated.

Mr. Speaker, in recent weeks we have heard the Opposition in this House continuously attack our U.S. neighbours on matters of foreign investment, defence sharing, and trade. While our new Government begins initiatives to get our country back to work through co-operation inside and outside Canada, all Canadians see is the Opposition "American bashing", rather than joining with us and working toward jobs and prosperity in this country. Many Canadians, including myself, are sick and tired of this action.
I suggest that most Canadians want co-operation with our good friend and major trading partner to the south. Due to the poor investment climate in the past, too many Canadians took their investments to the U.S. I challenge Canadians to invest in Canada. As well, rather than criticize foreign investment, why not get involved in joint ventures with investors from the U.S., Europe, and the Pacific rim countries who want to invest in this great country of ours?
Canada has prospered because of joint research with the U.S. in many areas such as health care, communications, and transportation, to name a few. U.S. advances in technology have helped in Canada's over-all prosperity, a prosperity which our new Government is attempting to restore, not with pessimism and contempt but with fairness, openness, and a willingness to work with our friends. This positive approach will not sell newspapers, but it will get Canadians back to work and at the same time keep Canada a strong and sovereign nation.

Mr. Speaker, I have been informed that CBC Radio has cancelled two more of the longest running programs on its AM network, namely, Identities and Anthology. subtopic: NECESSITY TO PRESERVE FOOD PRODUCING LAND
NECESSITY TO PRESERVE FOOD PRODUCING LAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Ethiopian crisis that wrenched the emotions of Canadians during the past year is one tragic example of the world's growing need for human food. Yesterday around the world 40,000 children
February 5, 1985

under the age of Five died of starvation. Today another 40,000 will die, and there will be yet another wave of tragic deaths from starvation tomorrow. Additionally, 70 million persons per year, roughly three times Canada's present population, suffer permanent and irreversible brain damage from a shortfall of protein.
In the face of that overwhelming and clearly demonstrated need for human food, Canada still does not have a widespread understanding or appreciation of the need to preserve our agricultural land. We are complacent in the false comfort that the world's hungry people are elsewhere, and that the problem is not ours. We accept the myth that Canada has an abundance of agricultural land. The truth is that Canada is diminishing its food producing capacity at such a rapid rate that a tragedy in both economy and nutrition is inevitable if we do not reverse the rate at which we destroy our food producing soil.
One-half of the original farmland in Ontario is now permanently removed from agricultural production. From 1971 to 1976, 200,000 acres of farmland in Canada's largest province were removed from agricultural production.

That "tell us what to do Government" of nightwatchmen, Ministers who fight amongst themselves, and a Minister of Finance who admittedly enjoys the support of the Prime Minister occasionally, has succeeded in creating so much uncertainty and confusion that the Canadian dollar has been driven below 75 cents.

With this obvious loss of confidence, will the Prime Minister undertake to get behind the Minister of Finance in order to remove those divisions in Cabinet so that some over-all, coherent direction can be given to economic policy?

speechtext: I should like to interrupt proceedings to advise Hon. Members of the presence in our gallery today of the Hon. Paul Schoenals, Minister of Energy and Mines of the Province of Saskatchewan.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. He will know that at this moment on foreign exchange markets the Canadian dollar is trading at 74.89 cents U.S. He will also know that in the past when the Canadian dollar softened, the Liberal Government made ordinary Canadians carry the brunt of that softening by increasing interest rates, including mortgage rates.
Knowing that an increase in interest rates at this crucial time would have a devastating effect in terms of investor and consumer confidence, will the Minister follow the traditional Liberal pattern, stand passively by, and allow the Bank of Canada to increase interest rates on Thursday?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased the Hon. Member has drawn attention to the fact that for some 21 out of the past 22 weeks interest rates in Canada have gone down successively, to the point that they are now down to a level which we have not seen for a number of years. That has done a tremendous amount to increase the confidence of Canadians and the expectations of increased improving economic performance.
We have watched while some changes in the U.S. dollar have put some pressure on the Canadian dollar in recent days, but I think the Hon. Member should not be too impatient. These are things that normally happen in a market.

Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House recall that the Prime Minister, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, and the Minister of Finance on many occasions indicated that after September 4 billions of dollars would move into Canada from outside, strengthening the value of the Canadian dollar as it built confidence. Could the Minister explain why that hasn't happened, why in fact the Canadian dollar is falling, and why there is little indication, as a result of that, that confidence is growing?

Mr. Speaker, I think there has been every indication that confidence in the country has grown significantly since September 4. We have seen close to 100,000 jobs created. We have seen retail sales increasing successfully in the months since then. There is no question in people's minds that this increased confidence is expected to continue and result in a very enhanced economic performance certainly over the months ahead and years ahead. The Hon. Member likes to walk around with a little cloud above his head. I think he should look around and see what is happening about him, before he asks these pessimistic questions.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board. Could he explain why 1,200 grain handlers have been laid off in Thunder Bay? At the same time, could he explain this terrible mismanagement by the Wheat Board? This type of lay-off is unprecedented. It is even more than those experienced under John Diefenbaker. I would like the Minister to explain this to the House.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is truly an important question. I wish they would get their act together. This morning the Leader of the Opposition referred to it as a strike, and this Hon. Member refers to it as a lay-off. I will explain why, very simply. It is a very serious situation for all of western Canada. We had a very bad crop last year. Our production is down 25 per cent. If he is accusing the Wheat Board of mismanagement, there are about 150,000 farmers out there who received final payments and were very satisfied. There are 150,000 farmers out there who believe that the Canadian Wheat Board has done a very good job of managing and selling farmers' grain, as we do on this side.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Minister, in his reply, has missed a very important point. He should know that grain handling which should have been done on the Great Lakes has been shifted to the West Coast. That has caused the type of lay-offs which took place. I want to know why there has been no use of winter rail movement. During the course of the last four years about 100 trains moved roughly one million tonnes of grain. Why has there not been a single train used for a single tonne of grain this year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me repeat it very simply for the Hon. Member. He makes a very good point. Farmers this year on the Prairies produced about 25 per cent less grain than they did the previous year. The reason for there being no eastern movement by rail is a decision of the Wheat Board. If he is telling me that he thinks the Wheat Board is doing a poor job, and if that is the position of his Party, then I think western farmers would be interested in knowing that. However, very simply, there is not enough grain to move. We would very much like to have surpluses of grain which we could sell. There would be winter movement of grain to eastern ports, and it would make jobs in eastern Canada. However, we simply do not have the grain to move.

Member appears to be making a claim that, because of something another Member did, the privileges of the House have been breached. On the basis of what he has said, I find that there is no privilege of the House that has been breached. I can find nothing else.
As I think the Hon. Member knows, my dilemma is that if he wishes to make a specific accusation or charge against or about the conduct of another Member, he is free to do so. That is his right. However, on the basis of what has been put before the House today, I must find that there is no prima facie case of the privileges of the House being breached.
It has been the custom for me to reserve my rulings on these matters but because this is a similar kind of situation to the one that was dealt with earlier, I thought it would be wiser if I simply indicated that what I had to say in the last case applies in this case. What we have here is a dispute about whether or not what one Member has done is appropriate. Any Member may feel as any Member wishes to feel about any other Member, but I hope that all Members know that an accusation or comments made about another Member of the House should only be made by way of substantive charge and that there are certain consequences that go with that. It would be entirely outside the bounds of the Speaker to find that a question of privilege had been breached as it was in the previous allegation. I must find, therefore, that there is no question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wonder if the Speaker could assist us by indicating the previous case to which he is referring. Was he referring to the case of the remarks made by the Hon. Member whose conduct is presently questioned against the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), or was he referring to another case?
February 5, 1985
I am speaking of cases on which I have already been asked to rule with regard to the conduct of Members.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. If I may, I think that there is a certain relationship which exists between Members of Parliament, their constituents and the public at large, so that-
Is the Hon. Member rising on the point with which we have already dealt or is he rising on a separate point of order? He knows that if he is rising on the same point of order, he may not do so.
On the same question, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps to clarify it and put it in proper perspective.

I did not mean to create a dilemma for the Hon. Member. I waited to see if others would rise on the question of privilege. No one else rose. My options were to reserve my judgment or to make it now. Since I knew what it ought to be, I chose to make it now.
