The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra):
That this House condemns the Government for its inadequate response to the growing financial crisis in the agriculture sector and for its failure to provide sufficient support and services to farmers who face severe economic difficulties in all regions of the country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest this morning when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) spoke on this very important topic. It occurred to me that for a Party that has been in power for 20 years to come into the House with a motion which castigates the Government for not acting on behalf of the farmers in the first five months of its mandate takes a lot of gall, as the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) said. It is also interesting to note that the Leader of the Opposition moved the motion, spoke to it and then disappeared from the House. If he was really interested in the well-being of Canadian farmers, one would have thought that he would have had enough interest to stay and listen to the debate.
I must give a good deal of credit to the NDP critic who had the common decency to say that this Government will be judged on its actions four or five years hence. That is a reasonable position to take. But for a Party which was in power for 20 years to do what it has done takes a tremendous amount of gall, and I find it offensive.
I suppose we can understand why the Liberals want to attack us and say that this Government has not been doing anything, since they did nothing for 20 years. I cannot think of one thing that could be considered an agricultural hallmark which was left by the previous Government. The previous Government and the previous Minister of Agriculture were very good at talking about the problems and the nasty situations in agriculture, but I defy anyone to name one thing which that administration was able to accomplish.
Someone might say Canagrex. Well, the Conservative Party understands the importance of the agriculture industry and knows the value of exports to Canadian farmers. Out of every dollar which a Canadian farmer earns, 50 cents comes from exports. In western Canada it is higher; it is probably closer to 75 cents out of every dollar. We know the value of exports.
February 5, 1985

The previous Minister, in talking about Canagrex, said that on a conservative estimate-he liked to use the word "conservative"; unfortunately, he never understood what it was to be a Conservative-we could look for $500 million worth of sales in the first year. What happened? There was about $17 million worth of sales, which is less than 5 per cent. A passing mark in most cases is 50 per cent, and Canagrex attained less than 5 per cent of what was anticipated. In many ways, that is lamentable. If it had performed there would have been no question that it would have had the full support of this Government and would still exist. However, there was no indication that it would perform and that was the problem.
It is obvious why the Official Opposition-and I wish it luck in its new role-does not want to talk about its record. The former Prime Minister asked why he should sell wheat in western Canada. Why would the Liberals want to talk about that? Who wants to talk about the fact that the Canadian farmer now pays more for energy supplies than the American farmer? Why do they pay more? Because the Liberals heaped tax upon tax. It is more expensive for Canadian farmers to go to the field than ever before, largely because of the tax which was imposed by the previous Government. It was that Government, through its irresponsible and totally reckless spending, that drove interest rates through the roof. That is the legacy of the previous Government. It is no wonder the Liberals do not want to talk about that record. It is obvious that is the reason they complain.
The Liberal Party says that it wants the Standing Committee on Agriculture to function. We do as well. Unfortunately, a year ago we could not get that committee to meet. We asked the chairman of that committee, in the House, when the committee would meet. We could not even get him to call a meeting. We had a meeting one night to discuss the Western Grain Stabilization Act, but had to adjourn because there was not a quorum. There was not a quorum because only one government Member, the chairman, came to the meeting. With that kind of dismal record, it is no wonder the Liberals do not want to flaunt it in public.
I do not think the time will be long enough to allow me to go through the items which this Government has managed to accomplish in less than five months. This morning the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) indicated that a lot of the things which had been done were not earth-shattering. We know that, but putting all of our initiatives together one can see the attitude which this Government has toward the resource industries in Canada. Canada has the potential to become a more powerful and influential country in agriculture if we pay some attention to the resource industries. Those industries include agriculture, forestry, fishing, energy and other resources.
One of the first things which happened when we formed the Government was that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) decided that the campaign commitment to reduce the amount of tax on farm fuels would be kept. That was done. A system was arrived at, with the help of the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall), whereby there would not be a rebate. That tax will not be collected and then refunded. We
Supply
hope that very shortly there will be a tax number available to farmers so that the reduction in the cost of farm fuels will be available when the fuel is purchased. That is a benefit to Canadian farmers.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) froze Seaway tolls. I admit that that is not a large saving-$1.5 million to $2 million-but it will help Canadian farmers. It is a step in the right direction.
We have addressed the policy on metric, on which the Minister spoke very well this morning. That policy will help Canadian farmers. It was an election promise and it was carried out. In addition, initial barley payments were increased in an attempt to put more cash into producers' hands.
I was disappointed during Question Period when one of the opposition Members spoke in very unkind terms about the job which the Canadian Wheat Board is doing. I find it unfortunate. The Wheat Board has just announced final payments which were very good and it should be given credit for that. The Wheat Board has been doing a good job.
It was also interesting to note this morning that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy)-who I understand is the Opposition critic for the Canadian Wheat Board-has not had enough interest in his position to ask a question about western grain since November 14. When he was Minister he did not know enough about the system to sign the forms which would allow cash advances to be made available to farmers. As a result, for the first time since I can remember, and I have had a permit book for almost 30 years, cash advances were late. Why? Because the previous Minister did not have enough organization about him to even get the forms signed.
That is the record of that Government in agriculture. It is no wonder that the Liberals do not want to talk about their own record. You would have thought that after 20 years there would have been a lot of things that they had done for agriculture. Why is agriculture in such bad shape? To the extent that government can have influence in this sector, theirs was a negative influence. We have to put up with what that crew left us.
On advance payments we moved as quickly as we could. Again this was not a large item but it provided relief for people with unharvested grain in the Peace River country. It helps those who have had an early snowfall and not had a chance to harvest their crops. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), along with the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelle-her), invoked the Meat Import Act. This was a major problem. Had we had some understanding of the cattle industry by the previous Ministers, we could have used this in the previous calendar year. Unfortunately there was no interest shown, it was left hanging too long, and it is this Government which will look after what we believe is some unfair competition from Irish beef imported into this country. Who is doing it? This Government and this Minister of Agriculture.

February 5, 1985
Supply
The Liberals talk about research. Sod is being turned today for the construction of a research plant. They cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. They cannot castigate us for cutting out research and say that it is a good deal to go ahead with these projects. We agree that research is important in agriculture, but at least give us credit for the fact that research is going ahead and has not been cut back by the Department of Agriculture.
There has been talk about Section 31 of the Income Tax Act. I believe the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty) has gone a long way in interpreting that section to give farmers the benefit of the doubt.
There was some concern expressed this morning over the Western Grain Stabilization Act. The Act has been in force for 10 years and we intend to amend it very quickly so there is an interim payment to producers for spring seeding. But do you know when the payment came out under the previous Government? In August. Big deal! There is no reason why the previous Minister could not have had the legislation amended in time for an interim payment to help the producers in their spring seeding. Why was that not the case? Because there was no interest in agriculture on the part of the previous Government.
Then we have the situation in southwestern Ontario with the tobacco industry. It is a very serious situation. Some of the Members opposite were here at the end of the last Parliament. They will understand the political shenanigans that went on at the close of the session. I happened to be here, and a totally political Bill came in. We had the tobacco growers up in the gallery and it would have been very easy to pass the same kind of amendment this Government passed before Christmas which would have given the tobacco industry some hope for the then current growing season. This Government moved, and we give the Opposition credit for supporting it and getting it through in a hurry. But it would have been just as easy for the previous Government to do the same thing.
The National Farm Products Marketing Council is in the process of holding hearings to see what they can do about a marketing board for tobacco growers if that is what they want. But it was this Government and this Minister of Agriculture who understood the situation and got things done.
You guys filibustered last year.

The Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) should be ashamed of himself. He is a learned gentleman. He knows very well the kind of politicking that was going on in his own Party. I had a chance to talk to some of the Members of the Government at that time and there was no unanimity among them on that issue. So this shows what can be done if there is some will and determination and a proper attitude on behalf of the farmers in this country.
Another thing we have done is reach an agreement with the protein oils and starch research plant in Saskatoon. The Hon. Member should realize that is a research project. The agreement is to provide ongoing funding for another five years. That was on the table with the previous Government but it never got
done. We took it over and in a few months we have been able to work out an arrangement so that they will have ongoing funding for five years. That is very much an agriculture matter and of benefit to Canadian farmers.
The Liberals talk about the Americans. Whether we like it or not, they are very, very important agricultural tranding partners of ours. One of the first acts of this Government was to sit down with the American Secretary of Agriculture and work out a process whereby we can meet with him once every six months to talk about agricultural trade matters. This is in sharp contrast to the previous Government. Whenever they went down to the U.S. they would insult them. That is no way to get along with your neighbours. All we are doing is going to the table in good faith and if we have problems we will sort them out. That is certainly a step in the right direction.
The Minister has established some farm finance review boards on an experimental basis to see what can be done for people in financial difficulty. He has also moved to reduce interest rates for some 5,600 farmers who are paying as high as 16.75 per cent.
What about the other thousands, Charlie?

Admittedly there are lots more. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) makes a very good point. There are lots of problems out there and it is virtually impossible for the Government to address them all. But if we have the proper attitude and do what we can in the areas where we have some responsibility, eventually it will have some effect.
The Leader of the Opposition says he has travelled, Mr. Speaker. Let me tell him that I would like to travel with him to some of the farming communities and see what kind of reception he gets as opposed to the reception Members of this Government would get, based on the treatment they have had in the first five months of this Parliament. The Hon. Member shakes his head. I will go with him. I will challenge any one of them. I will go to any farming community they want in this country and we will talk about what we have done in five months as opposed to what they did in 20 years. We will see who gets the best reception. I will take up that challenge with any one of them.
Any time in Quebec.

Any time. You set the date and I will be there. That is a challenge I would very much like to take you up on. Any time in Quebec. I would be happy to go to Quebec. I have been in Quebec many times and if you are a farmer, as I am, you talk the language no matter where you are in this country.
One of the first things the very distinguished Minister of Transport did was freeze branch line abandonment, Mr. Speaker. There will be no more abandonment until we have had a full hearing to make sure there can be no other use for these lines before they are torn up. No one here talks about that. They talked about a rate freeze this morning. Freight rates are going to go down next year largely as a result,
February 5, 1985

unfortunately, of a poor crop. We do not have the volume to ship and volume is a factor in determining the full rate. But that is even better than a freeze. The Minister did not stand up and take a lot of credit for the fact that rates are going to go down. He quietly said that if we put the freeze in it will cost money so we will let the rates go down normally and worry about it another year. That is certainly a benefit to the Canadian farmer.
Another thing which we take for granted, because it has happened so gradually, is that interest rates have come down about 2.75 per cent since this Government assumed office. Rates have come down every week, with the exception of last week when they went up a very small amount.
And next week.

If you are wishing some bad luck on us, you must realize you are wishing bad luck on the whole Canadian economy. I think you should be happy that they have come down.
There are many other things we have done. Something which affects western Canada and was very well received was the licensing by the Department of Agriculture of something called HY320. This is a new high-yield variety of grain. It was grown experimentally for the last couple of years and licensed last week. Again this is not earth-shattering and it will not receive a lot of national press attention, but things have been done on behalf of Canadian agriculture. So for the Official Opposition to come into this House with that kind of motion I find absolutely appalling. I suspect that people tuning in will also find it so.
Surely to goodness it would add to the debate and the demeanour of the House if we could have a balanced approach in this House. There are some things the previous Government did that I could give it credit for; but when hon. gentlemen get up in the House all you hear is gloom and doom and how terrible things are. The Leader of the Opposition says there is a strike at Thunder Bay. Another Liberal Member said that people have been laid off. Why are we not shipping grain from Thunder Bay? I can tell him that there are eight feet of ice there and how are we going to ship grain from Thunder Bay? That is obvious. You look like absolute fools.
I congratulate the official spokesman for the NDP on agriculture. He had a balanced statement. He criticized some of the things he thought we should be doing or where he thought we were going in the wrong direction. But he ended up by saying that the real judgment of what this Government is doing will come in four years' time. I am suggesting that if you look at the real consequences of the previous Government being in power for 20 years, they are obvious because we have some serious problems in Canadian agriculture.
I will conclude by saying that I will defend the Government's record with regard to Canadian farmers at any place in the country, on any platform, with any Member of either opposition Party, and 1 will be happy to do it. I think farmers
Supply
would like to know the record. I would very much look forward to doing that if anyone wants to take me up on it.
Our mandate is for at least four years. In that period of time we intend to carry out as many of our campaign commitments as possible. We certainly look forward to that opportunity. On behalf of Canadian farmers I look forward to doing what I can, as part of the Government, to ensure that that very important sector of the country is treated fairly. Those are the exact words that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) used. If we can treat it fairly it will certainly be a new and novel way of treating a very basic and important industry in the country as compared to the treatment it received from the previous Government.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the Hon. Minister's speech with a great deal of interest. However, he neglected to deal with some very specific promises made by some of his colleagues, including the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle). I have three points I would like to see clarified by the Minister.
First, the question of stabilization payments owing to Quebec hog producers. The $13 million, the cheque that was symbolically signed by the Minister of Public Works. Is the Minister prepared to inform the House today that he was indeed going to cash the rather bouncy cheque written by his colleague from Joliette?
Second, the $60 million promised Quebec producers to compensate them for damages suffered as a result of drought. Is the Minister prepared to undertake today that $60 million in compensation will be paid to Quebec producers?
Finally, I would like the Minister to explain the advantages of his dairy policy and justify the cutbacks he made in the Government's dairy policy, that his colleague, the Minister of Agriculture made in the Canadian Dairy Commission's policy, without prior consultation with Quebec and Canadian producers.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite familiar with the situation of pork producers in Quebec. To use the words of the Leader of the Opposition, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) is a very fair-minded individual. I am sure that with the good representation which we have from the Member's province and the attitude and reputation of the Minister of Agriculture, the pork producers in Quebec will be treated as fairly as is any other group of producers in the country. That undertaking was made prior to the election in September. That will be the hallmark of the Government. It will treat people in all parts of the country equally.
I cannot give the Hon. Member an answer about the drought because I am not totally familiar with the circumstances. I know that there was a drought agreement signed with the prairie provinces to maintain livestock numbers. That was one of the first things that the Minister of Agriculture did

February 5, 1985
Supply
after September 17 when we assumed office. I am sure that the people in Quebec will be treated as fairly as are any producers in any other part of the country.
With regard to dairy policy, the previous Government talked about a dairy policy but it was postponed and reviewed every year. I believe that the Minister has given the assurance that he is working to establish a new dairy policy by August 1. When we say that we will work with people, we will do exactly that. We sit down and talk to people. With that attitude and process I believe that an agreement can be worked out. The Minister of Agriculture has given the deadline of August 1 and we will do our best to ensure that that deadline is met.

Mr. Speaker, my question to the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board is with regard to Prince Rupert Grain Elevator No. 1. I know that he and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) have been working very hard to find ways to keep PRG No. 1 operating. The Price-Water-house study which was provided to the Canadian Wheat Board, the Government of Alberta, Prince Rupert Grain and a few others on February 1 is going to be considered on February 14 to see whether commodities other than wheat can be moved through PRG No. 1. Could the Minister give us an idea of how things look with regard to PRG No. 1 ? PRG No. 2 is about to open. The net loss of jobs in the Prince Rupert area will be very substantial if PRG No. 1 is closed down.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) raises a very important issue. We have had some conversations about this on a one to one basis and have sent some correspondence back and forth. He makes a very good case. If my memory serves me correctly, we stand to lose about 75 jobs in that area. We need about 100 people to operate PRG No. 1 and something like 25 are needed to operate the new terminal. There is grain in the new terminal on an experimental run-in basis.
The problem is compounded this year by the fact that there was not a good crop on the Prairies this year. At the very time when we have increased capacity on the West Coast, our exports will be down because we had a poor crop. I have had some conversations with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) and I can assure the Hon. Member that we will be happy to work with him and do everything we can to ensure that PRG No. 1 remains open. He makes a good case that the matter should be looked at with regard to some special crops such as alfalfa pellets.
The Government is committed to doing what it can to ensure that PRG No. 1 remains open. However, we must bear in mind that exports will be down because the volume produced on the Prairies is down. I appreciate the concern expressed by the Hon. Member on behalf of his constituents.

Mr. Speaker, does the Minister agree with the policy announced on December 21? At that time the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced that the disaster relief agreements which have been in effect for a number of years will be done away with. Through those agreements the federal
Government and the provinces shared on a two to one basis compensation for disasters such as drought and flood. The former federal Government had agreed to pay $16 million in addition to the $8 million paid by the provincial Government as compensation for flooding in northeastern Saskatchewan. The new Government only provided $8 million on a dollar for dollar basis. I believe that a federal-provincial agreement provided for $60 million of relief in southern Alberta and southern Saskatchewan.
My understanding is that the Minister of Agriculture plans to do away with that arrangement and make the federal Government and the actual producers responsible for disaster situations. The Minister knows how important the participation of the provincial Governments was in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Quebec this past summer. Does the Minister agree with the new approach of the Minister of Agriculture? Will he be supporting him in Cabinet on this matter? This will mean that the producers will have to put up dollar for dollar equally with the federal Government and that the provincial Governments will not make any provision for assistance in disaster situations.

Mr. Speaker, I can say two things to the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). When farmers or any other groups have problems due to weather, a good case can be made that there should be some assistance forthcoming from various levels of Government. The agreement which was worked out with the provinces was agreed to by the provinces. It was not a two to one agreement, as the Hon. Member suggests it should have been; it was an equal sharing of one to one. It is my understanding that the provinces accepted that. I have not received any correspondence from any of the provinces saying that they should have had more. I take it from that that the provinces are in agreement with the provisions that were worked out.
Second, we are all looking for ways to make crop insurance work better. Crop insurance is available to provide some assistance in those situations. If people choose not to buy crop insurance, both levels of Government have reason to take a hard look at providing assistance on an emergency basis. Providing crop insurance can be made responsible enough; it should be able to provide farmers with support and assistance in those situations.
The agreement was worked out with the provinces and they agreed to it. We are looking at ways to ensure that we can handle those situations in the future with crop insurance. Hopefully, we will not get into a situation where we must provide emergency aid, whether for drought or for excess water.

Mr. Speaker, I will start out in this debate today from the same position I took last night in the short intervention I made on the subject of credit during the debate in Private Member's hour. During the election campaign the Conservative Party made it very clear that it had a program that it intended to bring forward and pass this year. The measures behind that agricultural program

should be put before the House so that we can either commend or criticize the Government on the fulfilment of its commitments.
Let me read from a letter that was written by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) before taking office, which states what the Progressive Conservative Party would do about agriculture when it came to power. I will then comment on its fulfilment of those commitments. First:
A Progressive Conservative government will commit its share of the necessary funds in order to ensure completion of the municipal drains in Eastern Ontario under the E.O.S.A. Agreement.
I cannot comment on that commitment but I gather that the Government has taken action.
Second:
A Progressive Conservative government will establish an Agribond Program to provide loans at reduced interest rates to agricultural producers. A tax exemption for earned income on these bonds would be provided to attract investment capital to this program.
We have heard much about this approach but there has been very little action. If one is to believe the document entitled Tax Issues in Agriculture, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will not be particularly happy with the agri-bond approach. Although it is a promise, there is no commitment to fulfil it.
The third point is:
We will work with producers and provincial governments to establish a Voluntary National Income Stabilization Program for the red meat sector and any other non-supply management sector which wishes to take part. Where tripartite agreement cannot be reached, we will amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act so that payments will come when they are most needed and greater emphasis is placed on costs of production.
The Government has introduced some amendments to the Agricultural Stabilization Act. I suggest that even Liberals who are trying to defend their past programs will have to admit that the Government's approach to the Act follows its commitment. If we accept the legislation, the amendments will at least plug a few holes that are currently affecting farm groups.
The fourth point reads:
We will reduce the price of farm fuels by 20 cents per gallon by removing the 9 per cent federal tax and by not collecting the current excise tax.
While this measure has been implemented, the method is not quite the same as indicated in the letter. It is a rebate system instead of the reduction of the price of fuels. The actual amount of reduction has been put into place and the Government has fulfilled that promise.
Point five is:
In order to provide aid to the tobacco industry, we will immediately introduce a unique Bill which will specifically designate tobacco under the Farm Products Marketing Act.
That legislation has been passed.
Point six reads:
A Progressive Conservative government would look to expand the role of the Farm Credit Corporation to take into account the high cost of entry into
Supply
farming, high interest rates, high land values and low commodity prices. We would ensure that the allocation of interest subsidies reflects the need to assist those who have entered farming in recent years.
I do not think we could expect the Government to fulfil that promise completely in the few months that it has been in power. However, it is important to consider whether the Government really has a commitment to address that problem because it is a key factor in the situation in which the agriculture industry finds itself. It will be interesting to see how the Government approaches this very difficult problem.
Point No. 7 reads:
We will change Section 31 of the Income Tax Act, as it applies to farmers, to reflect the principles of equity, neutrality, simplicity, and certainty. In addition, the strong-arm and confrontationist tactics presently practised by the Department of Revenue will be immediately abolished and a practice whereby the taxpayer is treated openly and honestly will be instituted.
That is a very laudable position. Section 31 deals with part-time farmers. Again, the document of the Minister of Finance entitled Tax Issues in Agriculture deals with Section 31. If we are to believe what the officials in the Department of Finance are saying, I would suggest that it is unlikely that there will be any change to Section 31. While we have heard discussion about that promise, there has been no action and may not be in the future. We will have to review that commitment in six months' time.
Point eight states:
We will abolish the imposition of capital gains tax on the sale of farm property for continued agricultural purposes.
There is much rhetoric on this but no action. There have been ongoing suggestions for the establishment of a task force or subcommittee to study this issue, but that has not been set up as yet. Again, I would refer to the Minister's Tax Issues in Agriculture. There is not much hope that the Government will move to remove capital gains, if one believes the approach in that particular document. However, the Government has the opportunity to fulfil that promise in the next few months if it wishes to do so, and we will wait before judging the Government on that commitment.
Point No. 9 reads:
A Progressive Conservative government will commit its share of the necessary funds to ensure that the Ontario Veterinary College proceeds with the renovations required to regain full accreditation.
I am not aware of the progress made in fulfilling that commitment.
Point 10 reads:
A Progressive Conservative government would be very aggressive in dealing with subsidized agricultural imports. We would move to control these imports in order to offset their negative effects.
I believe that the previous Government has much to answer for with respect to this issue. In the last GATT negotiations, our negotiators from the previous Government managed to increase the amount of tariffs against our exports and decrease the amount of tariffs against our imports. The actual effect of the last GATT negotiations by the previous Government was to increase the competition for our products in Canada and decrease the competitiveness of those same products when they

February 5, 1985
Supply
were exported. We can support the present Government if it takes the appropriate action in this area in the future.
Point 11 reads:
We will amend the Advance Payments on Crops Act to double its cash advance levels. The present legislation only doubles these levels for Western grains. We believe all crops, in all areas of Canada, should be equitably treated in a government's agricultural policy.
Again, such a policy will be adequate and worth-while if it is fulfilled. The Government has indicated that it will do so.
Let us judge this Government in a couple of months. There are other promises too that this Government has made or did make before it took power and on which it has not acted. We have had considerable information and suggestions that the Government would deal with the Western Grain Stabilization Act. The Tories said that when going into the election and they said it when they first appeared in the House. Somewhere about the middle of November the Tories indicated it would only be a matter of a few days before amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act would be made. We are still waiting for those amendments, and both opposition Parties have indicated they would support such amendments. The Tories have failed to bring them forward.
The present Government also indicated it would do away with the abandonment of rail lines. I must say that, to their credit, the Tories have made that move. But they have indicated very little if any commitment to the action which they themselves have taken. It seems to me window-dressing rather than an actual commitment to replacing into service those lines needed to give the agricultural part of western Canada the kind of transportation service which it needs and which was removed by the previous Government over a matter of about 15 years.
This Government and the previous Government should beware of throwing stones. The Conservatives still have a lot of promises which they have not fulfilled.
They never will.

The commitments they are making now are ones on which they will be judged in the next few months and years.
As I mentioned before, the three promises made concerning Section 31 on agri-bonds and capital gains do not look too good, according to the report of the Minister of Finance.
They are dead ducks.

Some of the moves this Government has made have been against the interests of farmers. I can mention one specifically, one that was brought out before the agricultural committee yesterday. The services provided to seed growers have been increased by 400 per cent and 500 per cent by this Government in a recovery program. The inspection of meat and the inspection of plots for registered or certified seed doubled, tripled or quadrupled in cost in comparison with what
it was before. This is at a time when farmers can ill afford to have increased costs. But this Government has been one of the institutions that has increased the costs of farm production and made it a little more difficult for farmers to make ends meet at a time when the farmer needs every opportunity and every method possible to allow production and good, profitable returns.
I think that the Liberals particularly should not throw stones. They had 20 years of opportunity to solve the problems of agriculture. They had 20 years in which their Government ignored the problems. The Liberals did a lot of things about agriculture here, there and all over, some of which benefited the farmers marginally and a lot of which disturbed the farmers and caused some harm. The most glaring example was the elimination of the Crow rate, a guaranteed subsidy to farmers which they needed. This too was done at a time when they could ill afford any extra costs.
We should not be wasting our time on debating which Government is the worst, the past Government or the present Government. It is the sort of situation where we are fiddling while Rome burns. That is exactly the situation in which agriculture is finding itself today. There are thousands of farmers in disastrous situations who are on the verge of leaving the industry. It is time that we in this House, as a Government, as three Parties that have been elected to be responsible for what happens in this country, get together and put in place a global approach, an income security structure which would allow the farmers to produce. If they produce well, they will know that they will be able to meet the high freight rates which the previous Government instituted, inspection costs which this Government has established, and high fuel, chemical and fertilizer costs. If the farmers have the kind of income security structure that would allow them to pay for these things, we would no longer have to worry about band-aids such as stabilization and insurance programs, because the income security program would cover those kinds of possibilities.
One could start out by saying that the Government would be giving a fair price, a price that would include the cost of production for each and every one of the commodities the farmers produce. That obviously would be the most direct and the easiest way to solve the farmers' problems. If that is too difficult, then let us take these two programs, the Western Grain Stabilization Program, the agriculture stabilization program and a variety of other programs which are part of the prop-up system that we are attempting to make available to farmers, and put them all together. Let us approach this on a global basis and say that what is available to the farmer is a certainty and that if he works well, produces well, is efficient and uses the market in the proper way, he will survive and be able to provide a living for himself and his family. He will not go under because of the interest rates, because of the lack of credit or the high cost of machinery; he will produce as he should expect to produce and get enough for it so he can survive. That is the basis on which this House should approach agriculture, not on the basis of small band-aids which may help now but at some time will have to be reviewed and
February 5, 1985

replaced by a global structure which allows the farmer to farm well and make a living.

I have a question for the Hon. Member, Mr. Speaker. On several occasions we have raised the subject of Section 31.1 think all Members in the House agree that it is a problem as it is presently enacted in the present legislation. Could the Hon. Member give us his ideas as to a possible solution to that problem or his Party's solution to the problem?

Mr. Speaker, our Party has discussed this as I suppose has every other group of people interested in agriculture. I cannot say we have a particular position. We have, however, put forward a number of suggestions. We hope to have the opportunity to put these possibilities before the Government and talk about them.
The idea that Section 31 might harm bona fide farmers is most often raised as an argument against changing it. I suppose we should be looking at an increase in the minimum if we think it must remain in place. That is a decision which all of us in the House may have to make. If we think the limitation should remain in place, we will have to decide on its size. Many of my constituents have indicated that they would be happy with it remaining in place if it were raised at somewhat the same level as inflation over the years. As we all know, the $5,000 of a few years ago is a pretty small sum today. That is one of the suggestions which has been put forward and which we would like to discuss with the Government.
Also we should define in Section 31 a little better than have the income tax people what is a commercial farm and what is a viable farm. We have to recognize the needs not necessarily of young farmers but of beginning farmers. I have discovered in my constituency that many farmers 40 to 45 years of age are just now trying to get into farming. They thought they could get into it in three years but they have found that it takes from five to seven years. They are getting caught in that section. That matter needs to be discussed. I am not saying that we have a particular position on it, but we have a number of ideas we would like to put before the Government and to discuss.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member was with myself and others on a trip to Washington in connection with the United States program of what amounts to agri-bonds. I would like to hear his comments on whether he felt that that was a proper way to assist farmers in terms of their long-term capital requirements. Keeping in mind the experience in the United States, does he think we should do something different from agri-bonds, or does he think it would be important for a Commons committee to study the report on tax issues in agriculture which was tabled the other day so that we could obtain evidence in Canada with respect to agri-bonds? Also, in terms of Section 31, does he think that we should take this matter before a Commons committee?
Supply

I would think that a Commons committee with very specific terms of reference to deal with agri-bonds and Section 31, if possible, would be a good idea. What we need in this particular area is input from many people other than ourselves, because we become isolated if we stay in the House too much.
As far as agri-bonds are concerned, I recognize, as did all of us who visited Washington, that the biggest factor against the agri-bond program or the exempt bond program in the United States is the loss of money or funds to the Government over a long period of time. As Members of Parliament who were elected to govern Canada, not just one section of it, we have to look at that as a detriment to putting into effect the agri-bond structure as it was described to us in the United States. However, that program in the United States got money to the farmers when it was needed. I guess it was at a larger cost than we would like to expend. However, I am quite certain that we in Canada have the ingenuity to take that program and develop it in such a way that we do not have that loss. For instance, our Party's position on that is that it should be done at least in those cases where elderly farmers want to sell their land. Then the agri-bond becomes part of their retirement benefits. There are a number of such approaches. That particular suggestion was not made in the report on tax issues in agriculture. It is the kind of suggestion which needs to be made. This is the reason I think a committee or task force to study the matter and bring some suggestions to Parliament should be set up as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member concerning Section 31. When one reads the discussion paper, I think one begins to worry that Section 31 will be buried in a lot of bureaucratic mumbo-jumbo and that nothing will happen. That is my worry.
Would the Hon. Member and his Party be willing to suggest that at least when an audit is being conducted by income tax auditors, they should be forced to call upon an expert in agriculture to accompany them when they inspect the farm? Then they could come up with some concrete ideas and thoughts on whether or not a farm is capable of producing a profit, whether it is a viable farm or, in other words, in what category the farm should be placed. I have found in my riding that auditors would just arbitrarily place a farm in the hobby class, although they did not have the expertise to do that. Would the Hon. Member agree that that is the very least for which we should settle?

Mr. Speaker, I know the exact problem to which the Hon. Member referred. I have many of those people in my constituency as well. I think it is important that a definition be established, but I worry about establishing such a definition. I recognize that the Department of National Revenue has been inadequate in that particular relationship, in the use of that section in the past. It has been used mainly retroactively. I think that is the biggest problem. However, I am not at all sure that establishing a definition for farmers, for farming or for valid farms is what we want to do. Does it mean

February 5, 1985
Supply
that we do not think part-time farmers are making a contribution to the agricultural industry in particular areas? For instance, around Prince Albert there are many farmers who also work part-time at the pulp mill or in the bush. They are really productive people. To some extent they are attempting to build up their farms, but they are making a very good combined living. If they were unable to farm or not allowed to make that kind of living, they would probably move away, particularly people who work in the bush in the winter. They would not be able to make a living on the farm and the bush work would not be enough. We need to look at the whole structure and allow enough flexibility in it so that if decisions are made, they are not made to the detriment of taxpayers.

speechtext: Unfortunately the period provided for questions and comments is now over. We shall resume debate with the Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Brightwell).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-SUPPORT FOR AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate. The importance of maintaining a strong and dynamic agricultural industry has always been understood by the Progressive Conservative Party. We have only been in office a short time, and already we can point to a proud record of achievement in support of farmers across the country.
If we look at the history of support programs in this country, we find that the majority of federal agricultural legislation and agricultural institutions were established by Conservative Governments. The Canadian Wheat Board, the Farm Credit Corporation, crop insurance, the Agricultural Stabilization Act, ARDA, and the Prairie Grain Stabilization Act are all good examples of our concern for Canadian agriculture and the welfare of Canadian farmers. At the provincial level, the same holds true. Conservative Governments brought in most of the marketing boards which have done so much toward stabilizing farm income and bringing order to the agricultural market-place.
I want to make it clear, however, that these institutions and the legislation are only support mechanisms. They were never intended to interfere with farmers' personal freedom or their responsibility for their own success.
In my close association with farmers and in business life I am well aware of the harsh realities of agricultural life. Farmers know, when they enter the business, that there is no guarantee of security. They have to be careful. They have to be frugal. They have to work hard and live within their means because of the narrow margins, the traditionally poor returns on capital, and the risks of both natural hazards and the uncertain market-place. The market-place is no less threatening to farmers than flood, drought or frost. Each farm family must take primary responsibility for coping as best it can with these hazards. Farmers understand there is no escape from the harsh realities, no excuse for bad management. In short, farmers know that they must carry their weight, take their own risks and live with the consequences.
Every independent businessman must maintain that sort of attitude towards his or her enterprise. The federal Government recognizes, however, that there are some aspects of the agriculture industry that are unique. There is the vulnerability to the weather and to international political and economic forces, for example, all of which require Governments to adopt special support programs for farmers.
These support programs are not designed to guarantee every farmer a living, but rather to ensure there is an economic environment in which farmers may prosper. They also ensure that Canadian consumers have a continuing supply of high-quality food at reasonable prices. In addition, government support programs enhance the agriculture industry's contribu-
February 5, 1985

tion to the national economy, a contribution that is substantial, I might add. In terms of trade, for example, the agriculture industry contributes some $4 to $5 billion annually in surplus foreign exchange.
Federal and provincial Governments have adopted a wide range of programs to help the agri-food industry. In total, at the federal level, nearly $2.5 billion annually is spent on agriculture. In ballpark figures, this includes $60 million in stabilization payments, $300 million in dairy subsidies, $160 million for crop insurance, and that will be closer to $186 million this year, $250 million on research, $220 million on inspection and regulation, $650 million through the Crow benefit, and $110 million through the Western Grain Stabilization Act. Then there are the many market development programs, including advance payments for crops, which provide around $450 million a year in interest-free cash advances to farmers. There is also feed freight assistance to feed-deficient areas.
There are also the federal-provincial agricultural subsidiary agreements under which we encourage market development, technology transfer, and improvements to the natural and human resources of agriculture. Designed in co-operation with the provinces, these programs are tailor-made to deal with problems that are specific to each region of the country.
Let me return for a moment to crop insurance. It is one of the best examples of federal and provincial Governments and the producers co-operating to provide support where it is most needed. While most areas of the country enjoyed reasonable growing conditions last season, the Prairies were hit by a combination of serious drought in most areas and floods in some areas.
Last year more than 118,000 farmers insured 37 million acres of crops, for a total of $3.4 billion. Premiums, with the producers paying half, came to $331.2 million. Payments to farmers for 1984 crop losses exceeded $521 million. In other words, for an investment of about $165 million, farmers ensured a cash flow of more than $521 million. Needless to say, most of that went to prairie farmers hit by the drought, $257 million to Saskatchewan, $205 million to Alberta, and $29 million to Manitoba.
At the same time, a Government must remain flexible to deal with special situations. The severity of the conditions on the Prairies last summer warranted extra action, and we entered into agreements with the provinces for a Prairie Livestock Drought Assistance Program to help some 30,000 livestock producers affected by the drought. This program pays $48 per head for cattle and $10 per head for sheep in zones designated as being severely affected by the drought, and $30 and $6 per head in moderately affected zones. Producers will share some $63.5 million in benefits, with the federal Government paying half of the costs.
Similarly, we are sharing with the provinces the cost of flood support programs that will provide about $15 million for farmers in northeastern Saskatchewan, and we are working out details for a similar program in Manitoba. A program for
Supply
1983 forage crop losses in Quebec has already been announced.
Crop insurance has been successful because it is the kind of program that farmers share in and understand. It is voluntary and it is contributory and leaves the farmer free to make his decision based on his own management style and resources.
Producers have indicated they would prefer that same system for stabilization programs. Amendments have recently been introduced to the Agricultural Stabilization Act to reflect that view. Even a cursory examination of the present stabilization program shows its flaws. Farmers do not know how much support they will get under the program until long after they have made their production and marketing decisions. It is a case of justice delayed is justice denied. Furthermore, under the present program, farmers often receive their stabilization payments just at the time when market prices are recovering. That is not only bad timing, but it can also distort production decisions.
The new program, which Members will be able to discuss in detail before the Agriculture Committee very soon, will be prompt, it will be voluntary, and it will provide an improved level of support without costing the federal Government much more than the current program. In short, the new approach to stabilization will be in keeping with the whole thrust of this Government's fiscal strategy to spend smarter, not more. That same approach will be reflected in amendments we propose for the Western Grain Stabilization Act. An interim payment in the spring will help farmers with cash flow at the critical time when they are making their planting decisions.
To summarize, it is clear that farmers understand their fundamental responsibility for the success of their operations. Secondly, an extensive system of supports is already in place. Finally, new, innovative programs and policies are being developed by this Government to provide more effective protection and encouragement for farmers, but in a more economical fashion.

Mr. Speaker, very simply, let us go to what this debate is all about. It is designed to spur this Government into some form of action. The time has come for all the paperwork, all the rhetoric, all the grand promises and exaggerated commitments to come to an end and for the Government to do what it was elected to do, which is to take some action on behalf of farmers who are facing some very immediate, very critical short-term problems.
It is all right for the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) to talk about the need for some far off global strategy to solve ultimately and finally the problems of the farmers. However, at this very moment, farmers in various regions of Canada are facing very specific and immediate problems and they are looking to this Government to provide some leadership which, until this point, has been totally lacking. It has not been lacking because of any great sins of commission; the Government just has not done anything. It

February 5, 1985
Supply
has not begun to address the issues about which it spoke with great flourishes during the summer. Government Members said that they were going to be the great helmsmen of the agricultural community. We need only look at some examples to see what has really happened.
We should look at the paper put forward on tax issues in agriculture by the Department of Finance. What does it say about all the commitments the now Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made last summer? It says that they will not really work. We have heard all this gobbledegook from the Department of Finance before. We know that it can find all of those answers to questions over which members of the Conservative Party rose in wild indignation during our tenure in government. Here they are coming up with exactly the same thing. There has been no change. The same paper has been put forward by the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). He is a Tory, I believe. The paper is in his name and it contains such things as why agri-bonds will not work and why capital gains cannot be established. The most effective critique of Mr. Mulroney's promises come from his own Minister of Finance.
We cannot expect the farmers, who have been waiting in grand expectation since the summer for Mulroney and company to get their act together, suddenly to pick up this paper that was produced by the Minister of Finance and say-

I beg the pardon of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). I would not in any way want to denigrate the Prime Minister by calling him by his last name.
I would say that the Hon. Prime Minister has one more time been befuddled and betrayed by his own Minister of Finance who contradicted everything he has said in this white paper. Either that is so or it is the Minister of Finance who is really telling it as it is and it was the Right Hon. distinguished, esteemed gentleman who occupies the seat of the Prime Minister who does not know what the hell he is talking about. It is probably closer to the point that the Prime Minister simply made a commitment that he had no intention of fulfilling. He was up on that platform about which most farmers know a great deal because they know exactly what cows produce. That
is the platform on which Tories stand when they make agricultural promises.
Let us look at another very critical issue, Mr. Speaker. The Government was going to deal with the immediate cash crisis of the western farmer. When our Leader spoke in Prince Albert, he said that the very first piece of legislation that would be brought into the House would be an amendment to the Western Grain Stabilization Act so that western farmers would have cash in their hands on discretion either before the new year or after the new year, depending on their tax positions.
This House opened the first week of November. The "associate-we're-not-sure" Minister responsible for the Wheat Board-and I will return to that in a moment-has said consistently, "any day now, mafiana". I think he took his parliamentary lessons from the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) who keeps making promises-

speechtext: That's right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-SUPPORT FOR AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Oh, there is one of our distinguished agricultural representatives from the City of Toronto sitting in the corner.
The fact of the matter is that the Government had every opportunity to bring in that change to the Western Grain Stabilization Fund at the very beginning of this Parliament. It is now the first week of February. Where is that change? As a result, many farmers do not know what choices to make in terms of purchases of fertilizer and in terms of making their commitments to the future, because they do not know what kind of refund they will receive from that fund.
For Government Members, it is simply called action, Mr. Speaker. It is simply called deciding that they are now a Government and are not here to act Henny Youngman or Lenny Bruce and do a stand-up comedy routine in the House of Commons every day. Government Members should be trying to provide some leadership on major agricultural problems. We know that nothing is more important than getting cash in the hands of the farmers at a time when they need it. That time, Mr. Speaker, is now. Farmers need that money now, not after some consultation and not after another white paper.
I can only suspect that the real strategy of the Conservative Government is to help the pulp and paper industry. All of this is designed to bring employment back to the pulp and paper industry. No Government in the history of this country had produced so much paper read by so few people containing so little that no one knows about what they are consulting.
A constituent of mine went to the Queen's Printer and asked for one of the Government's consulting papers. The Queen's Printer said that that would cost $18. We know with whom Government Members are consulting. They are consulting with their own bagmen and friends who can afford to pay that kind of price. They have no interest in consulting with the general public. They are not prepared to hold public hearings.
February 5, 1985

They are not prepared to use House of Commons committees. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) will consult by taking a piece of paper to his friend in Toronto in the dark of the night and slipping it under a door, thereby saving his friend $18. That is the kind of consulting that is going on. Government Members are not prepared to get into a public debate.
We on this side of the House are using our time in opposition to bring those issues forward so that the Canadian public will know exactly what it is that they can expect. It is interesting to note that the Ministers are so seriously committed to this issue that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) have not quite found it possible to spend this day in the House listening to agricultural issues.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-SUPPORT FOR AGRICULTURE
speechtext: That's because they are meeting with farm groups. You never, ever met with them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-SUPPORT FOR AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
It is about time that Ministers of this House learn that their first responsibility is to this House.
I would like to correct the Hon. Member. I was in his riding this weekend and met with farm groups there. The Hon. Member had better go back and check on those groups because they are not too happy with what he and the Government have been doing.
We are beginning to sense some of the reasons why the Government is behaving in this manner. I would like to raise a particular point which came to light yesterday in very interesting testimony before the Agriculture Committee. We have always paid proper respect to the necessity of having a Wheat Board with its own Minister with his own independence and his ability to provide for the direction of an agency which is very clearly responsible for much of the important work done in western Canada. I would have to say, as would some of the western Conservative Members if they were allowed to speak, that we have always been concerned that the Department of Agriculture has had designs on the Wheat Board. It did not like the fact that the Wheat Board was deciding about and representing the marketing and export interests. We discovered yesterday that the new Government, which says it is so reflective and representative of western interests, has now substantially altered the relationship between the Wheat Board and the Department of Agriculture. According to the organizational chart, the Wheat Board now reports directly to the Deputy Minister and Minister of Agriculture. The poor Minister of State for the Wheat Board is stuck way off in the far left-hand corner behind a dotted line, the meaning of which we are not sure. It probably means that he gets to see the Minister of Agriculture at least once a month. I think that that is the definition of a dotted line.
This is no laughing matter, Mr. Speaker. This is a very serious matter for western Canada. It means that the Department of Agriculture has taken responsibility for the Wheat Board and has basically made the Minister of State for the Wheat Board into a kind of a glorified Parliamentary Secretary. The Wheat Board is under the thumb of the Department
Supply
of Agriculture, a Department which has its own very different interests. I can testify to the fact that those interests are not necessarily ones which will promote the activities of the Wheat Board.
This is a very serious change and one that totally dilutes and diminishes the powers and responsibilities of the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board. There is no longer any point in asking him any questions because he is reporting back to the Minister of Agriculture. We confirmed that by questioning the Minister of Agriculture, who we know is an honest and upstanding gentleman and one of the few such gentlemen on the front benches. Yesterday he said, "Yes, indeed that is the case". He said that he is basically running the show.
I think that that kind of merger carries with it very serious implications for the Wheat Board's ability to make judgments required in order to carry out its responsibilities. To compound the problem, we also found that the grains group is reporting to the Deputy Minister of Agriculture. God forbid! There is a serious problem in that organization. It means that the Wheat Board has seriously compromised its ability to represent western grain interests with regard to marketing exports. It would be far more beneficial to western Canada if the Wheat Board were more closely tied to the area of export marketing, because that is where the action is. That is where the responsibility resides. I hope that the Right Hon. distinguished, esteemed, plenipotentiary Prime Minister-and I hope that satisfies the Hon. Member for Mississauga South-will take a look at the organizational chart, which probably escaped him because he is so busy rehearsing his comical lines, and recognize that he has not lived up to the responsibilities of the Prime Minister, which is to run the Government and to ensure that all regions are effectively represented and that the agencies serve their purposes.
A major and fundamental change is taking place in the United States with respect to agricultural policy. The policies of Secretary of Agriculture Block and the new budget which was put forward by President Reagan basically wipe out all farm subsidies and supports. That is the proposal which Congress is considering. It has an important implication for Canadian wheat growers, and especially grain growers, because Secretary Block has said that he will get the money from the farmer by marketing in the most ruthless manner possible. We have seen the results of that. We have seen how the Americans have used their tremendous capacity in the grain export market to keep prices low or to drive the prices down.
Canada is in a situation which is compounded because of the problems of the existing drought and the loss of export markets. We are now in the position where we should be playing hardball with the United States. However, from what we have experienced so far, this Government does not want to play hardball with the Americans. In fact, it likes to play cream puff with them. The Government is not prepared to knuckle down and deal with the United States. We have seen time and

February 5, 1985
Supply
again that when the United States President says, "Jump", our Prime Minister says, "How high?"
Western farmers will be faced with intense competition from the U.S. agricultural department, which will use the wonderful techniques, subsidies and marketing devices to keep the international grain market at a low level and to flood and dominate that market. Ultimately, Canada will be forced to make a tough response.
I am pleased to see that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) is in the House because, at least in a titular way, the responsibility is on his shoulders. He will have to ensure that Secretary of Agriculture Block's pronouncements do not come true. We would much prefer to have the Canadian Wheat Board more closely aligned with External Affairs' activities in the trade area, to ensure that our western commodity interests are properly protected.
If we looked carefully at the trade paper-that grand design which amounted to 32 pages of regurgitated old material-we could ask ourselves what it said about the grain trade and the commodity markets. In Winnipeg we use a wonderful Ukrainian expression which means "there is nothing there". There is nothing which would enable western farmers to recognize that this Government is taking seriously the necessity to address the very major turbulences in international grain developments.
The Wheat Board does its job-it markets. But the number of countries in which Canada has been marketing has been shrinking substantially over the years. That is partly because we are being driven out of foreign markets. I would also suggest that it is partly because we are not taking full advantage of the opportunities which many of the new specialty crops provide in the export area. It is very important that another trade paper be developed which will deal specifically with the strategy, intentions and programs which will support extended export markets for commodities, specialty grain crops and staple grain crops.
When in government we did our part. We changed the grain transportation legislation to ensure that there would be an efficient and effective transportation system. A lot of decisions are still outstanding because of those changes, and we will be watching with interest to see what the Government intends to do when the report is received on the method of payment question. I hope it will learn how to take a stand, because that Party did not take a stand during the several months of debate on that legislation. The Government will be required to make a decision, and it is very important for that decision to be aimed at expanding our export market.
In addition, this Government has not taken a stand on the question of minimum compensatory rates for canola crushers who have severe problems in western Canada. The problem is one of uncertainty. If a decision is not made, then the ability of the canola crushing industry to provide for new capital investment, to develop markets, and to look at new opportunities as an industry will be left in limbo. Once again, it is simply a plea for action.
Decisions have not been taken because the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board has been cut adrift and no longer has agency responsibilities. Agriculture has been pushed aside because of consultation papers, grand dreams and promises. In the meantime, there is a lot of hurt and a lot of uncertainty, which will ultimately work to the detriment of the entire Canadian economy.
I would like to mention another issue, which is vital to western Canadian agriculture, upon which we expect action. It is the major problem of soil erosion and water. The Liberals established a major water commission which is due to report. The previous administration also held a number of negotiations and consultations in which the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) was very effective. We have seen year in and year out the inconsistency of the grain growing belt which is affected by major changes in climate, particularly the availability of water. There are approximately 200,000 hectares a year which are taken out of major grain production because of soil erosion in the southern parts of Alberta, the central and southern regions of Saskatchewan and parts of the Province of Manitoba. In order to respond to the predicament of our major grain growing area we will need capital. It is the responsibility of the federal Government, in co-operation with the provinces and industry, to provide the dollars which are needed for major water projects. The Government cannot avoid that responsibility. Yet the Minister of Finance and his cohorts are preaching the theology of deficit reduction. They do not recognize that governments from time to time must invest. Government has a direct public responsibility to invest in better production, improved facilities and infrastructure. In western Canada there is no more important a priority than investment in the area of soil and water development. But we cannot do this with nothing. It is very important that the point be made now before the budget comes down in several weeks. We must ensure that the Minister of Finance and his Cabinet colleagues include a provision for investment in major water projects in western Canada so that we can begin to stimulate the provinces in order that they will be able to respond. That is the kind of public expenditure which I think all Members of the House can endorse. It is an effective investment, designed to increase production and ensure protection for western farmers and the agriculture industry. I hope that those who are so quick to latch on to the new theology, the neo-conservatism in the prescriptions of the Minister of Finance, will, at least in this area, recognize that this kind of pound foolish philosophy has no place when it comes to dealing with these problems in western Canada.
In this opposition motion we are simply saying that this is the Government now. Members opposite cannot keep blaming the past and rewriting history. They are the ones with the responsibility, they must make the decisions. The western Canadian farmer is waiting for those decisions, and so are we.

Questions or comments?
February 5, 1985

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-SUPPORT FOR AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my friend gives a fine speech in opposition and he will be there for many years. Would he agree that, in the international sphere, the EEC is really the bad boy when it comes to agricultural subsidies and international marketing? The United States will retaliate nose to nose, and Canada will be in a very difficult position because we lack the financial clout to compete with those big boys. That is primarily because of the huge national debt and the amount of revenue necessary to service that debt. Why did the Liberals run up the deficit so high? It is now affecting our ability to make the investments he talks about. Why did they so consistently kick the United States in the shins and insult them in every possible way? As a result, we are now having difficulty reaching agreement with them. Why did they not sign an international agreement giving a base price for wheat? Why did they increase the input costs of agriculture so high? I am referring to fuel costs and transportation. Why did they not enact plant breeders' rights so that when the new varieties come out it would have a multiplier effect on our economy? Why was there no action for over 20 years on soil erosion and loss of agricultural land in western Canada? Why, for 20 years when they were the Government, was nothing done?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-SUPPORT FOR AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would certainly agree at the outset, and that is where the agreement will stop, that there is a very major problem with the EEC in international marketing. This is particularly true in coming to grips with the subsidies and supports they provide. We would be far more effective if we had some joint strategy. But what I have been trying to say through the course of my speech is that there was nothing in anything the Government has done, particularly in its trade paper, to indicate it was addressing the issue. It did not demonstrate what the Government was doing, what kind of intervention it was prepared to make, or whether it was endorsing or adopting the same kind of response the Americans were going to make. We are simply saying that the opportunity was there and if the Government did not want to use it, then it had better come out with another paper right away so that we know where it is going.
The Hon. Member has engaged in a form of mental gymnastics which I find is peculiar to the acrobatic school, causa Conservatus, which relates everything back to the deficit. The fact is that government expenditures provided job training, major innovations in transportation, and export development. They were used for major investment in regional development. I remind the Hon. Member that one of our initiatives which this Government, to its credit, has continued to support, was the establishment of the economic regional development agreements. They incorporated a number of agricultural agreements with the provinces. In my own Province of Manitoba we signed a $23 million agricultural agreement to provide for new research and development. There were new initiatives in water research and development and irrigation projects. We also signed a $200 million program, part of which went for a major restoration of the Port of Churchill, so that there was an alternative deep sea prairie port. We will have the opportunity tomorrow in committee to determine if this Government is going to fulfil the requirements of that agreement. For the first
Supply
time in the history of western Canada we took the decision, under that agreement, that grain cars would be manufactured in western Canada.
We used the power of expenditure, which he was so concerned about, to do exactly what I was talking about. We were investing in the future. We were putting in place the kind of research and development infrastructure which would allow the agricultural community, through those projects, to improve itself. That is why we are now in real danger of committing some serious mistakes given the approach the Minister of Finance takes when he says you cannot afford to spend on anything. In fact, in the economic statement of November, the Government added substantial new charges for farmers. Some $32 million was added to the cost burden of farmers. In some cases, in provinces like Prince Edward Island, charges have increased from $15 to $50 for the inspection of potatoes. This comes at the very time we are saying it is important to try to reduce costs. The Minister of Finance is adding to those costs, adding to the burdens of the farmer, not trying to relieve them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-SUPPORT FOR AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the Hon. Member's speech, as I did to the speech of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) this morning. What does he propose we should do with that section?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-SUPPORT FOR AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat intrigued by the Hon. Member's question. He should really he asking that question of his own Minister of Finance. The position of our Party is that we are going to be very interested to see what the answer is. It is quite true that a number of Members spoke to this issue. Our Government indicated we would set up a consultative group to look at it, and now what has happened is that we have had these grand promises for legislation. This goes back to our basic thesis that you cannot make promises and then, all of a sudden, do a double flip-flop and say, "We are now going to study it". It is now back in committee for examination and we think it is very important that the Government take a stand. Let us see the colour of the eyes of the Minister of Finance. Then, my hon. friend, our critic on agriculture, will be more than happy to respond.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very pleased to answer the question. I find that the Member for Mississauga South has not outgrown old habits. Like an old dog he still plays old tricks. He has not quite got used to the idea that he is now a Member on the government side of the House. In this Parliament the Government is responsible for coming forward with the proposals. Member was listening, which I know he does raptly to everything I say, he will have heard that we did suggest that it is time that the Government got on with business and brought the stabilization fund forward, which could have provided close to $800 million of new cash flow for western grain producers. We made a very clear commitment to provide for an immediate cash flow to enable farmers to start their plans under the stabilization fund.
All we get from the Government is promises, promises, promises. That makes a good title for a Broadway play but it makes a lousy agriculture policy. The whole thrust of our motion is to say that there is a new Government now and it is about time it recognized its responsibility. It is about time it made decisions on these commitments. It does not do much if, at the same time as it is reducing taxes on excise fuel, it is adding service charges that end up costing the farmers more.
