speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is their ignorance of agricultural problems that brought about the national landslide that reduced their numbers from 980 to 162, while we have 579 Members across Canada, including this Parliament. Ask anyone, that is what producers are going to tell you, including hog producers.
We have been listening to practically everything that is being said about our hog producers. The subject came up in connection with the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), who was absolutely right in doing what he did, and he still is today. Hog producers across the country, and I know what our own producers are saying, will tell you they are well aware there is a major problem with the United States, and if it is dealt with too hastily, we might be hit with export restrictions, and that is something our hog producers want to avoid. I think we will be able to find a political solution to the $13 million question. Not a solution of confrontation, as you have always
February 5, 1985

advocated for much too long-which explains why we have reached the point where we talk about two Opposition parties here. A policy of consultation, that is what it says in the document of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), and that is a document for consultation. Pay close attention to the last paragraph on page 67: "The Government expects to hear from all interested individuals so as to know their views on these issues concerning the tax treatment of the agricultural community, in light of this document and of the principles contained in the Agenda for Economic Renewal". That's it!
Mr. Speaker, my riding is predominantly agricultural. There are dairy producers, hog producers and sheep producers. They know the agricultural community is experiencing difficulties. They want to hear what Hon. Members have to say about the real problems in agriculture. We all know what those problems are: a problem of overproduction, a problem of increasingly difficult exports caused by worldwide surplus production, a problem of surplus equipment, and a problem of indebtedness compounded by steep financing charges.
Today we are debating the issue of financing. Mr. Speaker, I wish all Hon. Members could have been in Washington where, in a non-partisan approach, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), for instance, and my colleague from Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) played an active role in the discussions in an attempt to find sound solutions to various agricultural financing problems. And after three days in Washington, there seemed to be unanimity, a consensus to the effect that we should not earmark less money for agriculture. All parliamentarians agreed that funds have to be set aside to help some categories of Canadian farmers. The idea was to find the most effective formula, the most profitable, rather than pick one at random only to admit later on that we made a mistake. We were there to draw inspiration from the American experiment. It is a new program.
When the Ministers of Agriculture attended the federal-provincial conference, there was no way to benefit from that American experiment. Now we can, and that is why the agribond program might be altered, solely with a view to finding the best way to finance farmers, particularly those who are just starting out in the business and others who are facing difficulties.
It is because there are so many of those farm producers in my constituency that I spend the greater part of my time here trying to identify the problems, trying to find with them what those problems are exactly, trying to identify them and find the most adequate solutions.
Farmers also are prepared, Mr. Speaker, to go beyond the mere question of farm financing. They know it very well because they have experienced and are still experiencing problems left over by the previous administration, the problem of too large a deficit, of too much government, a government that too often meddles with their lives as with the lives of all Canadians. They too are prepared to make sacrifices. They
Supply
did not resolve to complain just for the sake of complaining. They want us to help them find a long-term solution, with government action aimed not only at solving one immediate problem but at solving a long term problem. And the long term problem, Mr. Speaker,... I hear again the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) who is trying to interrupt me rather than making a positive contribution in this House! They know the problem is related to their production costs. If he calls on the milk producers in his constituency, they will all tell him the problem is related to production costs. They would like to get a price close to their production costs, the everlasting problem. They will not have anything else to tell him.
Mr. Speaker, the only way is to proceed through consultation, ongoing consultation as this Progressive Conservative Government has been doing for a number of weeks, trying to get the best answers by way of consultation. This Progressive Conservative Government has been using a new approach to the question of farm financing. A co-operative approach, with an attitude conducive to closer work between the various parties involved, including the Provinces which must be taken into account, as I say to my Liberal friends.
[DOT] (WOO)
At this moment, the Farm Credit Corporation is involved in financing programs in several Provinces. It is interesting to note that such programs are generally directed at helping young farmers go into business or expand their operation. We are directly co-operating with provincial financing programs in British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Quebec, Nova Scotia and Ontario.
The officials of the Farm Credit Corporation are constantly looking out for new methods to increase the level of co-operation. They are experts, and I often urge my constituents to call on those experts and seek their advice. The 20 per cent of farm producers who are in difficulty can often find the solution to their financing problems simply through an orderly and intelligent discussion with the Farm Credit Corporation experts.
The Farm Credit Corporation has persistently set as a major goal for the coming year the putting into place of new programs that will help farmers in real need in a more aggressive and better adapted way.
There are indeed a great many farmers in my riding. They call me on the phone, they write to me and they are prepared to sacrifice almost anything to survive these difficult times. If there is anything I want to say about the part the Government should play in farm financing, it is that we have worked very hard since the election to help farmers. Those who were stuck with interest rates on their loans of more than 16 per cent- more specifically 16.75 per cent-saw them reduced to 12.75 per cent per year a few days ago, which was certainly a step in the right direction; these farmers know now that this Government has made agriculture one of its top priorities.

February 5, 1985

This Government has been elected and given the mandate to consider problems with a fresh look and from a new point of view. I can assure the House that our Government has the firm intention not to shirk its responsibilities. We have helped farmers finance their operations and we will continue to do so, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to repeat what I feel is the major message the Government is trying to convey to the Canadian people: with your help, we can improve the well-being of the Canadian people.
The Government expects all interested parties to express their views on tax issues related to agriculture in light of this document and of the principles put forward in the economic statement. Mr. Speaker, I have asked for 1500 copies of this document that I intend to send to all farm producers within my riding.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise to speak to this opposition motion indicating the inadequate response to the growing financial crisis in the agricultural sector and identifying the Government for its failure to provide sufficient support and services to farmers who face severe economic difficulties in all regions of the country.
I am fortunate to represent a constituency in Canada that has a substantial number of farms, to be precise, 1,200 farms, of which 50 per cent are cattle ranches, 30 per cent are in various field crop opeations, 10 per cent are in fruit and vegetable growing, and 10 per cent are in specialized and mixed farming.
I am not going to make a speech today, but instead I shall reflect on three or four issues facing the agricultural sector that I feel are of particular importance today.
When you look around the world today, Mr. Speaker, and you recognize the trends internationally, you see that farming

February 5, 1985
Supply
communities in Europe, often heavily subsidized, are competing now directly with Canadian exports. In many cases those crops and products are so heavily subsidized that fair competition does not exist any longer. We see the situation in other countries, such as Argentina. Argentina in a sense is dumping its wheat on world markets, prepared to sell it at any price, not so much that Argentina is in the wheat sale business but it is in the business of obtaining foreign currency. The much needed American dollar in that part of South America motivates its pricing system for grains.
When you consider that in the United States today the Government is determined to protect a number of its sectors to subsidize heavily its agriculture sector, we face a very difficult international trading community when it comes to agricultural products.
Here at home with a new Government there is one concern that overrides all others, namely, that of the deficit. I am not confident at this point that the necessary support and assistance will be given to ensure that not only viable agriculture continues in Canada but, more important, that family farm or family ranch in western Canada continues as a viable producting unit. I see us as being at a crucial point today as a result of the financial crisis where we will be making decisions in the next number of weeks that will determine whether agriculture in Canada goes the way of the family farm or the family ranch or whether it goes in the direction of large-scale corporate agricultural business.
In terms of the future of Canada, it seems to me that it would be appropriate for the Government to take steps that would ensure that the family operator remains a viable food producer and not take steps that would inevitably see the rapid drift into the hands of corporate agriculture where we would have large commercial farms perhaps run by breweries, oil companies or petrochemical companies with very little interest and commitment, if at all, to the real agricultural community.
I have been fortunate enough to be part of a New Democratic Party action group on jobs. We have been touring the country over the last number of weeks. We have been to all parts of Canada, from Atlantic Canada to western Canada, to central Canada, through Ontario and Quebec, and if there is one thing that has been made perfectly clear at every single session, whether held in rural areas, in small communities or in large metropolitan areas, it is that there is a profound interest and a deep concern for what is happening to agriculture today.
What about farm bankruptcies? They continue to increase year after year. In 1980 we had about 200 farm bankruptcies. In 1984 we had about 600 farm bankruptcies. In 1985 it is predicted that in excess of 1,000 farms will experience bankruptcy. Those numbers, when you consider the number of farms in existence, may not be particularly problematic, but we should recognize as legislators that this is only the tip of the iceberg. For every farm that actually experiences the bankruptcy proceedings and the personal horror attached to that, there are hundreds and hundreds and thousands more farmers who are simply giving up. People simply give up and
walk away because they can no longer make a living from the operation.
The Farm Credit Corporation informs us that 39,000 farms at the moment are facing serious financial difficulty. Nearly
2,000	farms are on the brink of financial collapse. That is why we are here today. That is why the Opposition has decided that it is appropriate to discuss the seriousness of the situation in an effort to encourage government Members to use whatever powers they have with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to ensure that the necessary steps are taken. We can no longer afford to do nothing. We can no longer afford only to consult and discuss the situation. For years and years, as I recall, farm groups representing every possible area of the country and every possible sector of the agricultural community have been making their concerns known to Members of Parliament and to the Government, past and present. The problems being faced by food producers today are not a mystery to anyone. The problems are clear and, perhaps more appropriately, the solutions are relatively clear.
I became a little disconcerted when I received a discussion paper on tax issues in agriculture from the Minister of Finance. I, like all of us, am very interested in the taxation system as it touches the agricultural community. Yet, when I read this recently released report, page after page, I did not see any particular conclusions. I did not even see any real options provided. I saw three or four options provided, but they say that two will not work or will cause all kinds of problems and that they are not sure about the other one. I am not particularly encouraged by Section 31, which has profound influence in my constituency. Half the ranchers and farmers in my constituency are required to seek income off their operation. They have been harassed unbelievably by the Department of National Revenue. These people are now considered to be part-time farmers when some of the ranches have been in the family for three generations.
One of my most saddening experiences as a Member of Parliament, in my brief career here, happened the other day when I visited a small cattle ranch. I suspect that traditionally it would be running 250 to 300 head of cattle. It was run by a young family with three children in their early teens. Both the husband and wife had grown up on ranches, one on that ranch and another on the neighbouring one, as had their parents and their grandparents. They had just lost the family ranch, despite relatively sophisticated management practices and good equipment. They had worked for 12 months of the year, probably 18 hours a day. The entire family had worked-the mother, father and three children. They lost the ranch. The bank decided that it was appropriate to take over that operation. The tragedy was that if that family had mismanaged its operation, if it had not put up adequate hay, or if it had not looked after its cattle properly and some disease or whatever had infested the herd, that would be one thing. However, the family lost that ranch because of interest rates, an item over
February 5, 1985

which it had absolutely no control but over which the Government has control.
I noticed an article in The Globe and Mail the other day which was headlined: "Farmers are experiencing the worst time since the 1930s". On the opposite page it read: "Bank profits in Canada the world's best". On one hand our financial institutions now rank among the most profitable in the entire world, and on the other our farmers are experiencing financial difficulties like they did in the 1930s. What is the Government doing about that? In my estimation-and I know certain Hon. Members opposite would disagree with me-the Government is not taking any steps to reduce the deficit.
Just today we have seen the Canadian dollar dip below that important psychological level of 75 cents. I am afraid that the natural response of the Liberal Government will now be taken by the Conservative Government and interest rates will be increased to bring up the value of the dollar. I want to indicate that if that is the response of the Government to a decreasing dollar, which has other problems attached to it, it will be one of the most devastating moves the Government could take because of the fragile recovery that is out there. Farmers across the country welcomed a change of government. That Government promised to do a number of things. Farmers had said, "I suppose nothing could be as bad as it is now with the Liberal Government; we have nothing to lose". When Hon. Members opposite and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that the new Government would do certain things, there was a sense of hope. I suspect that, to a certain extent, that hope still exists. However, if interest rates go up next Thursday and on successive Thursdays, we will see not 1,000 bankruptcies in 1985 in the farming community but substantially more. I suspect hundreds of thousands will just walk away from operations to which they had dedicated their entire lives, as had their parents and grandparents before them. That is a very critical point. I must say that the discussion paper of the Minister of Finance is a disappointment. I personally-and I know it was the case with my Party-was certainly hoping for much more action than that publication suggests.
We must take action to reduce interest rates. I know the Government has an aversion to taking action to reduce interest rates. 1 guess it is quite content to spend hundreds of millions of dollars week after week to buy up our own currency to buoy up interest rates. That is an expenditure which I guess people do not mind.

As the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) just indicated, where they own their farms. That is the kind of Canada we would like to see. Barring a lack of interest or a lack of commitment to reduce interest rates across the board, there are other alternatives. The agri-bond alternative is one to which all Parties agreed at one time. It is something worth looking at. That is why I was disappointed when I read this. I do not think the Government will now move on agri-bonds, unfortunately. Originally we suggested that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act could be reintroduced as another method. While that worked back in the 1930s and the 1940s, I realize that it would have to be modified to work today. However, it is an option open to us now. As I said, not many months ago all Parties agreed to at least look at it seriously. I would like to see that initiative taken by the Government again.
I should like to refer to the whole matter of the set aside program. I want to remind all of us-and particularly Hon. Members opposite-that in the United States the Farmers' Home Administration has been authorized to set aside without interest for five years as much as 25 per cent of the debt owed by farmers in distress, up to a maximum of $100,000. Private lenders willing to write down a portion of loans to reschedule repayment obligations can apply to the Farmers' Home Administration for a guarantee on the remaining outstanding debt of up to $400,000 for operating credit and $300,000 for real estate. That Government recognized that it had to do something to help farmers who lost equity in their operations and that one way to do it was to set aside a certain amount of the debt, to be dealt with at a time when the farm was more of a producing unit. That is another alternative.
We have to look at something else, which is very serious for those of us who are interested in cowcalf operations or feeder operations. We have to look at introducing some type of beef stabilization program based upon the cost of production. A stabilization program based upon the averaging of prices does not help many people. Today, when the prices for beef are in fact lower than the cost of production, making that into a major guiding factor will not be of much help. A beef stabilization program to help provide that kind of support would enable the family farm or ranch to be successful.
I do not suppose there is much hope that the new Government will reconsider its position on Canagrex. Time and again the Minister of Agriculture has said that Canagrex is history in this country, something of the past, nothing to do with the present, and certainly nothing to do with the future.
Let us look at what Canagrex did over a very short period of time. Up to October 31, 1984, the total expenditures to set up Canagrex were $2,659,000. Canagrex arranged $16 million in sales and had an additional $100 million in sales that it was planning to wrap up by March 31, 1985. It had found and developed $160 million in sales in that short period of time. By the way, those figures are taken from Hansard where the Minister was answering a specific question.

February 5, 1985
Supply
If there is one thing that Canada must do, not only in agriculture but in other areas, it is to seek out and develop new markets much more aggressively. Never before has international competition been so difficult and yet important for Canada.
People in the farm community thought that Canagrex could play a very important role in certain areas. Some sectors were doing an excellent job. They were marketing our agricultural products extremely well. By and large, as in other areas of our economy, that was and continues to be a weak point. Canagrex was one of those operations that could have supported a lot of agriculture in Canada, particularly the newly developing agriculture where we are developing new crops and export potential.
I am a little hesitant to hark back to the old Government, but when you look at some of the deals we got under the last GATT agreement you, have to laugh. Our negotiators are out there to negotiate a great deal for Canada. I hope my Liberal colleagues will find some humour in this. Our negotiators managed to raise the tariffs on a whole set of our exports. That was supposed to help us, but I could never figure out how that would work. They reciprocated and said that we would lower the tariffs on all imports. That is not the kind of negotiation we were hoping for when they were negotiating on agricultural commodities, but so be it.
I want to close today, after having had an opportunity to say a few words about the problem facing agriculture, particularly in western Canada, by saying that the critical aspect is our shipping rates. Canada is the second largest country in the world. We have to ship many of our products a long way. That is why we fought so hard to keep the Crow rate to assist western grain producers.
The other day I happened to come across some information regarding the transportation costs on a case of corn being shipped out of Ontario. It cost $1.36 to send that case of corn to Japan. When the corn leaves here, it goes through the port of Vancouver and on to Japan. To send that same case of corn to Vancouver costs $1.63. In other words, it costs more to send it to Vancouver than to send it to Japan. It will cost 76 cents to send that same case to Germany. However, it will cost $1.22 to send it to Newfoundland. One of the critical areas in which we must work, if we are going to support a viable agriculture sector, is in the re-examination of transportation charges on agricultural goods.
I hope the Government realizes the seriousness of the situation. Opposition Members made the case today that we have a financial crisis in our agricultural community. Unless something is done very quickly, we will see the beginning of a massive demise of agriculture, more particularly of the family farm and family ranch.

Mr. Speaker, I certain enjoyed the speech of the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). He made a lot of points and stressed the serious nature of the agricultural community today. Is he aware of the cost recovery programs that were announced in the Wilson economic statement of November 8? Also, is he aware of a letter that was sent to different organizations involved in the marketing of food products, especially the potato industry in my Province of Prince Edward Island and in the Province of New Brunswick? The proposal, to be made effective on April 1, 1985, less than two months from now, is for an inspection fee of 33 cents per hundredweight to be set on all table stock potatoes for human consumption shipped out of Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick.
In Prince Edward Island the average crop yield is about 200 hundredweight per acre. This means that the inspection cost would be $66 per acre. The average potato farmer on Prince Edward Island grows 200 acres of potatoes. Therefore, he is looking at something around $13,000.
A seed inspection is also proposed of $25 a hectare for field inspection. That works out to $11 an acre. In my province, the Province of Prince Edward Island, 86 per cent of potatoes are grown as seed potatoes. However, less than 50 percent, probably 42 per cent, are sold as seed and the rest go into table stock. There could conceivably be a double inspection fee. Approximately 40 per cent of the production on P.E.I. would be subject to these proposed fees. That will involve $77 or $78 an acre.
That letter was read to me last night by the chairman of the P.E.I. Marketing Board. I read it back word for word to see that I had my facts straight. It was signed by the Deputy Minister, Mr. Quesnel.
I wonder how the agricultural community in my province could survive that sort of a huge price increase. The present cost of producing potatoes in P.E.I is six cents a pound. We get
4.5	cents a pound FOB P.E.I. so we are already selling them
1.5	cents below the cost of production. No farmer can operate very long that way. This is very discriminatory. If you look at the production of potatoes in the Province of Ontario, you see that most, potatoes grown are sold within the Province of Ontario. Therefore, they would not be subject to the inspection fee. Areas like Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick are totally reliant on shipping out of province or to the export market. I see the Minister is now here. I hope that he will make some comments regarding this very serious situation about which I am speaking.
If the Government goes through with this measure, this to me would spell the end of agriculture as we know it in the Province of Prince Edward Island. I would like to hear the Hon. Member's comments on that.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the elaborate question put by the Hon. Member, as well as his deep concern. Those same letters went out to people not only in Atlantic Canada but to people across Canada generally. I believe that the Hon. Member's calculations were $77 or $78 per acre. is to spell out the end of agriculture as a viable sector in Prince Edward Island.
A similar argument can be made as well for a whole number of areas. I tend to concentrate on the beef industry in which the situation is the same. That is why I say that we have come to a critical point at which we as legislators must make a decision regarding whether or not we want agriculture in P.E.I. and other areas as well to continue as a viable way of life. By failing to take action on a whole variety of fronts, including the financial front, agriculture will begin to fail across the country.
Countries like Japan, for example, have taken it upon themselves to say that they believe that agriculture is critical for their countries. Self-sufficiency in agriculture is their goal. We have no goal like that. As a matter of fact, if we are to identify a goal based upon the point made by the Hon. Member, the goal would be to phase viable agriculture in Canada out of operation. That is why we must decide whether or not potato growing in P.E.I. will continue as a viable economic activity. From our point of view, we must take steps to ensure that it will continue.

I know that members of the Liberal Party, and particularly the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, have a lot of trouble with consultation. When the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry was Minister, he knew all the answers. He did not have to consult with anyone because he knew all the answers. We have no difficulty with that. These are policy positions that we discussed during the election campaign. We hope that some other suggestions will come forward to allow the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to put in place the kinds of policies that are up to date and will suit the continuing viability of agriculture in the country. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry had the audacity to speak of the Western Grain Stabilization Fund and to chastise the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board for not yet bringing in an amendment to the Western Grain Stabilization Act. If the former Minister who was responsible for this Bill had accepted our amendment at that time, an amendment which was requested unanimously by opposition Parties, we would not have to amend the Bill. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, the Minister at the time, would not heed that suggestion. The present Minister is now forced to deal with the situation, and he will deal with it. He will meet that promise and it will be put in place before the farmers plant their crops this year. You can be assured of that,

February 5, 1985

Mr. Speaker. The situation on the Prairies is desperate and many farmers are depending on payments from the Western Grain Stabilization Fund for cash to put their crops in the ground this year.
I agree with the statement made by the Hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) that we in government must look seriously at alternatives that will assist us in keeping family farms all across the country viable. I know that when this Party sat down before the election and deliberated on policy, it had that in mind. If we look at the record of this Government, in the short time that it has been in office, we will find that the Government has adhered to more promises in that short time than did the last Government with two Ministers in five years. I could go through the policies which have been implemented, but other Members have already done that. Those policies have assisted in lowering the cost of production to many farmers. It has given farmers an opportunity to be optimistic about being able to meet their payments and to put in their crops in 1985.
There is much financial distress as a result of what happened from 1970 to 1981. During that time land prices increased dramatically and the cost of production increased together with inflation. The cost of production perhaps increased even more rapidly than inflation. At the same time, the price of agricultural production was also increasing. When the 1980s arrived, Governments were not prepared for the results. Interest rates skyrocketed as agricultural prices leveled off, and in many cases became depressed. At the same time, the cost of production also increased rapidly. Lending institutions, including the Farm Credit Corporation, were lending money to farmers based on increased equity. The lending institutions were looking through rose-coloured glasses in anticipation of higher prices for farm products. Those higher prices never resulted.
We cannot blame the farm managers for getting wrapped up in the escalating war for land, or for trying to plant crops and getting a reasonable return. The best advice in the country was telling them to do that. If we look at the statistics, the farmers who produce most of the food in the country are also the farmers who are most capital-intensive. In most cases they are farmers who have the potential for getting into financial stress if everything does not work properly.
We know the difficulties in agriculture. Even those who live in the cities probably had fathers or grandfathers who were in agriculture. We know that weather can be a determining factor. It is a factor which will not be found in other businesses. Nothing is more distressful than to see a farmer being removed from his property. He is also removed from his home. There is something good about being close to the soil. When farmers are forced off their land, it is a very serious matter. In a lot of instances the land has been in the family for a number of generations. Factors which are different from those in the business sector come into play. Even the best managers can experience bad weather and be forced from their land because
they are unable to make payments. Governments have a responsibility to bring forward the kind of policy which will keep farmers viable across the country.
Many Members have spoken about the difficulties in getting our produce into world markets because the United States and the EEC are presently battling over markets. But Canada has a good record in that regard. The Progressive Conservative Government of the 1960s was able to get into the markets in Russia and China and lead the way in getting Canadian agriculture products into those markets. We now have preferential treatment when our grain is moved into those markets. Even in these competitive times, the Canadian Wheat Board was able to sell, in the last four or five years, all the grain which our transportation system has been able to get to port. It is an excellent record upon which the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) will build.
I am pleased that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) has dealt with the Farm Credit Act and has allowed the farmers who were locked into high interest rate loans to bring them down by 4 per cent or 5 per cent. That practice is assisting more farmers in Canada than the set aside policy of the United States. I believe there are 8,000 farmers in the United States who are being assisted, but there are 6,000 or
7,000	farmers in Canada who are being assisted by that policy. If the Minister's policy can be adopted, it is worth looking at. I believe a number of banks are responding to it.
There was a situation in my constituency in which a cattle feedlot company was in financial difficulty. It went to the bank to seek a solution to its difficulties. The company had $1 million in debt which it had accumulated over the past three or four years because of stabilized cattle prices and increasing costs. After much deliberation, the bank was able to work out an agreement. The bank bought half the shares of the cattle company and set aside half the loan for five years. The company will pay the loan on the other half. That will allow the company to get back on its feet and, hopefully, to repurchase the shares which are now owned by the bank.
Financial institutions are now prepared to write down some farm loans. Perhaps the farm financial review boards which are now operating on an experimental basis in two counties in Ontario will find the same kind of success as they bring farmers in distress together with financial institutions in an attempt to work out solutions which will allow those farmers to stay on the land. subtopic: ENERGY-VENTURE OILFIELD PROJECT. (B) NEGOTIATION OF OFFSHORE DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCE OF NEWFOUNDLAND
ENERGY-VENTURE OILFIELD PROJECT. (B) NEGOTIATION OF OFFSHORE DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCE OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to discuss a question that I asked on November 26 and the answer I received from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). It concerned two very important matters, that of the Venture project off Nova Scotia and the Hibernia project off the coast of Newfoundland. I was really not satisfied with the answer the Prime Minister gave, and since then the situation grows increasingly more confused with respect to the Government's policy on these two very important projects. These projects have the potential to create and maintain many jobs in the hard-hit Atlantic region of this country where unemployment is a tremendous problem and getting worse all the time.
The main reason this lack of direction exists, Mr. Speaker, is that there is no intention on the part of the Government to put forward a fiscal regime for these two very important projects. I asked the Prime Minister, concerning the Hibernia problem, when the agreement would be signed. What was the situation? He referred in his answer to an accord being worked out. An accord, Mr. Speaker, had been worked out. It had been agreed to in June, 1984, between the then Leader of the Opposition, now the Prime Minister, and the Premier of Newfoundland. This was an accord between two buddies who supposedly are so enamoured of each other that they feel there is no problem in reaching an agreement. We had that accord in June and a second one in December, but we have yet to get the agreement. Where is this agreement? Supposedly the federal Government offered the Province of Newfoundland everything it wanted, yet there is still no agreement. This is taking far too long. The Government is not coming forward with answers to the question regarding Hibernia. It sloughs it off completely.
On a subsequent occasion we asked for the environmental impact study, and the Prime Minister said he would provide it. In response to subsequent questions from my colleague from Corner Brook someone in the Government said that there was not an environmental impact study and that all COG LA had was a draft of the environmental impact study. We are not getting answers to these very important questions. If these two accords between the two Parties are so unanimous, why do we not have an agreement at this stage?
This situation has now extended to western Canada. The federal Government said that there is now an era of compatibility and there will not be any problem reaching new agreements with the three western provinces. Yet on two occasions the deadline set by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) has been extended. The Minister has undertaken to use the energy sector as an engine for growth. I agree that this is an extremely important aspect. If the Government looks upon this as an important aspect, why has there not been more of a concerted effort to reach agreements with the Province of Newfoundland and the three western prov-

February 5, 1985
Adjournment Debate
inces? There have not been negotiations with the Province of Nova Scotia since the agreement with the Province of Newfoundland was signed. There has yet to be a meaningful dialogue with the industry.
With these things in mind, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Government to make more of a concerted effort to bring these very important questions to a meaningful consensus.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-VENTURE OILFIELD PROJECT. (B) NEGOTIATION OF OFFSHORE DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCE OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it bothers me greatly to see the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) so perplexed. I am going to set his mind at ease right now so that he will have a wonderful evening and can relax.
On the matter of the Venture gas field, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) explained when the Hon. Member raised the question of the fiscal regime last November, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) has advised the companies associated with that important development that the Government will ensure a favourable fiscal regime that will not place companies at a disadvantage in any way vis-a-vis anything that might have been available in the past.
It is incorrect to infer, as the Hon. Member did, that there is no fiscal regime in place to govern the Nova Scotia offshore. The Canada Oil and Gas Act, which was passed by the Thirty-second Parliament in December, 1982, clearly establishes an offshore fiscal authority which is applicable to Nova Scotia. That Act provides for a 10 per cent basic royalty on the value of production, as well as a progressive incremental royalty on 40 per cent of new profits over a certain level.
In addition to this framework, last June the previous federal Parliament passed the legislation formalizing the Canada-Nova Scotia agreement for offshore oil and gas resource management and revenue sharing. I am sure the Hon. Member remembers that, and he is probably briefing the Member for Hamilton East (Miss Copps) on that very agreement. That agreement provides for a mechanism to ensure that Nova Scotia receives, with the exception of federal corporate income tax, all revenue from adjacent offshore activity until the province's per capita fiscal capacity reaches 110 per cent of the national average.
That answers that part of the question. There is a fiscal regime in place for Nova Scotia. In addition, and of most importance, there are provisions for Nova Scotia to substitute for the present agreement any agreement made by the federal Government with another province which would be more favourable to Nova Scotia. The agreement, to be reached shortly with Newfoundland, and relevant provisions from forthcoming agreements with the western provinces, could be considered under this most favoured province clause of the Canada-Nova Scotia agreement.
With reference to Newfoundland, may I say at the outset that the Government remains firmly committed to the formalization of the Atlantic accord with Newfoundland. There is no problem with it and things are going swimmingly, as they might say in Newfoundland. We are very pleased with what is happening with the agreement.
Since our Government assumed power, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has met twice with her counterpart in very fine meetings. There is not the acrimony that we saw with the previous Government. As a matter of fact, both sides have shown a determination to work co-operatively and expeditiously to Finalize these very complex and vital arrangements. I do not believe the Hon. Member would want them to rush and make a poor agreement that would be detrimental to Newfoundland or to the people of Canada.
I can tell him that a third meeting between the Newfoundland Minister of Energy and the federal Energy Minister will take place this Thursday. We are most hopeful that great progress will be made. The negotiations that are taking place now are being held in the best of atmospheres. Progress is being made, and I know Canadians will be very pleased at the results which I am sure we will hear in the not too distant future. In the meantime, the people in Newfoundland, the oil and gas industry and Canadians as a whole will benefit from all the agreements that the Government is carrying out in a very conciliatory atmosphere.
I must say that my constituents and people to whom I have talked throughout the country are happy to see that. They do not want to see the provinces fighting with the federal Government as we have seen over the last number of years.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-LA REGIE DES RENTES DU QUEBEC- CANADA PENSION PLAN-INJUSTICE TO PUBLIC SERVANTS IN THE NATIONAL CAPITAL REGION
SOCIAL SECURITY-LA REGIE DES RENTES DU QUEBEC- CANADA PENSION PLAN-INJUSTICE TO PUBLIC SERVANTS IN THE NATIONAL CAPITAL REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 6, 1984, I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) a question to which I did not receive a reply, a question that is of considerable importance to the region as it concerns the Regie des rentes du Quebec and the Canada Pension Plan. My question was that the Government of what used to be "la belle province" has changed the regulations for the Regie des rentes du Quebec and lowered the pensionable age to sixty, provided the individual is no longer in the labour market and agrees to a certain penalty, a decision that affects, and I think Hon. Members will agree, thousands of public servants in the Ottawa-Hull region.
I read, because this is quite subtle, that "if an Ontario resident works all his life on the Quebec side, he is eligible for benefits under the Regie des rentes du Quebec, while a Quebec resident who has worked all his life in Ottawa or Ontario is eligible only for benefits under the Canada Pension Plan which does not operate in the same manner as the Regie des rentes du Quebec in this respect."
In other words, Mr. Speaker, this means that there has been injustice. I do not know whether this flaw could have been
February 5, 1985

detected or even existed when the plan was established. It seems that when the Province of Quebec decided to set up its own plan, it was to be identical to the Canada Pension Plan. That was one of the basic criteria established at the time.
Previously, 1 put this question to the former Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) in March 1984. I could not do so before that time because what used to be "la belle province" changed the legislation on the Regie des rentes du Quebec as of January 1, 1984. The injustice apparent here is something we do not find anywhere else, where people in border areas are concerned. That is why 1 would like to know whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and especially the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), in the course of conversations with their provincial counterparts, intend to find a way to remove this injustice, these inequities for contributors to the Canada Pension Plan and the Regie des rentes du Quebec.
Of course, a person who lives in Quebec all his life and observes the rules and regulations laid down by the Province of Quebec and who wants to stay in Quebec, but is in a position where he has to work in Ontario all his life, cannot take advantage of such benefits as the province provides for its fellow Quebecers.
Mr. Speaker, that is why I asked the Minister whether he was willing to deal with this flaw in the Canada Pension Plan and the Regie des rentes du Quebec. We must remember that this was done unilaterally, and that there were no consultations, as far as I know, between the authorities of what used to be "la belle province" and the federal authorities with a view to amending this legislation. So this was done unilaterally, and the question I want to put to the Minister is whether he is willing to meet with his provincial counterparts to talk about this very considerable flaw that has developed over the years, especially during the past year, with a view to eliminating this injustice, these inequities that are affecting hundreds of thousand of federal public servants, Ontarians working in Hull and residents of Hull working in Ontario, and get rid of this very discriminatory situation. That is why 1 wanted to get an answer from the Minister. It is not because there is any loss of money involved, because I hope the Canada Pension Plan reaches the same conclusion as the Quebec Pension Plan, because we put more people in the market and it does not cost the Treasury a cent more, for the simple reason that a condition, a penalty is added, I think it is 5 or 6 per cent between sixty and sixty-five and at sixty-five there is no increase in the normal rate. The cut remains until you are no longer drawing a pension. And the other condition too, the criterion as I said, is that the individual must no longer be in the labour market.
So I hope ... I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mrs. Bertrand), the Member for Brome-Missisquoi. I hope she will be able to
Adjournment Debate
provide an answer that will satisfy the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are caught in a situation that could easily be remedied.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-LA REGIE DES RENTES DU QUEBEC- CANADA PENSION PLAN-INJUSTICE TO PUBLIC SERVANTS IN THE NATIONAL CAPITAL REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would like the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer (Mr. Isabelle) to note that in his comments he used the word "injustice" many times as well as the expression what used to be "la belle province", and I want to point out to him that the province of Quebec is still a "belle province". In reply to his question, I can say that we are indeed aware of the amendments made by the Quebec Government to the Quebec Pension Plan, making the payment of pension benefits available at age of 60, with an actuarial adjustment. You explained it quite well. This change, which has been in effect since January 1, 1984, allows contributors to the plan to receive early retirement benefits provided they leave their job. The pension of those requesting their benefits before age 65 are reduced by 0.5 per cent for each month remaining until they reach that age. It is very important to note that, because of the actuarial reduction factor, the amount of the benefits paid out over the lifetime of those who opt for early retirement is equivalent to the amount of unreduced benefits which would have been paid to them had they waited until the age of 65 to retire.
Since the establishment of the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans in 1966, there have always been differences between the two plans. Early retirement is only one example of this. However, in spite of these differences, the two plans have always been considered basically similar.
As for determining under which plan the benefits should be paid, the rules are quite simple. Someone who has contributed only to the Quebec Pension Plan is protected by this plan wherever he or she resides. By the same token, someone who has contributed only to the Canada Pension Plan is protected by this plan, wherever he or she resides. For people who have contributed to both plans, there is an agreement between the Canada and Quebec Governments dealing with the payment of benefits. Under this agreement, a contributor to both plans who resides in Quebec at the time of his application for benefits is subject to the provisions of the Quebec Pension Plan. On the other hand, if he resides in a Canadian province other than Quebec at the time of his request for benefits, he is subject to the Canada Pension Plan.
I find it quite fair that all those who have contributed to a plan can equally benefit from it. This is why I do not see any need to amend the rules for the payment of benefits.
As for the question asked by the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer, I believe that his suggestion would be quite welcome in the context of the reform of the Canada Pension Plan which we supported during the election campaign and which would recognize provincial jurisdictions.

subtopic: MULT1CULTURALISM-IMPLEMENTATION OF COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS. (B) ABELLA COMMISSION REPORT-DATE OF PRESENTATION
MULT1CULTURALISM-IMPLEMENTATION OF COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS. (B) ABELLA COMMISSION REPORT-DATE OF PRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 14 I asked the Minister of State for Multicultural-ism (Mr. Murta) a couple of questions dealing with the report of the Special Parliamentary Committee on Visible Minorities, and I followed with a query about the awaited report from Judge Abella. Admittedly and understandably the answers I received were quite tentative. I requested then the opportunity to speak further on the matter. Now, about two and a half months later and more than twice as far into the life of the present Government as we were at that time, it is appropriate to consider the record of the Government to this point. Also it is appropriate to inquire about the possibilities of early action and to press for that early action which various members of the Canadian community, visible minorities of all sorts, have been hoping for so long.
The report Equality Now focused on the need for action in a great variety of areas, but I want to focus particularly on the employment recommendations. Of course, the Abella report contained concerns about equity in employment. That was its main focus.
The record of the Government to this point has not been very reassuring. The recommendation to establish a Department of Multiculturalism never had the support of the Conservative Party. Presumably it will not be a policy of the Government now. That is to be greatly regretted because it is important to have someone responsible, a minister with a department and substantial resources, in order to achieve the ends for which so many Canadians hoped. Whether we will have a standing committee perhaps is not entirely in the hands of the Government. It is likely that recommendations 25 and 26 of the report will not be acted upon. One is tempted to conclude that we are likely to see the same contrast between rhetoric and reality which characterized preceding Liberal Governments ever since the policy of multiculturalism was enunciated in 1971.
Another area of concern is that of appointments to various boards, commissions and other offices which the federal government control. An assessment of the actions of the new Government, whatever the protestations of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) have been, again have been disappointing. There were precious few appointments of people from the visible minorities, from the ethno-cultural diversity of the country. However, I am pleased to see that Francophones and women fared rather better in appointments.
Recommendation 21 of the Commission still awaits action. The activities of the Minister of State for Multiculturalism vis-a-vis the National Association of Japanese Canadians in the last few weeks, focusing on recommendation 33 of the report, again arouse concern. There is no readiness to negotiate a very narrow concern about redress for that aggrieved
community. I only hope that my expression of concern proves to be unjustified.
These particular decisions by the Government in past weeks leave one concerned about the extent to which there will be action in areas of employment. Surely employment is ultimately the area in which there has to be action if the report Equality Now and the Abella report are to mean anything at all to Canadian society in general.
The various recommendations in Equality Now call for the early establishment of a five-year program by the federal Government with regard to the various corporations and institutions that it was involved with, a well formulated five-year program designed to achieve a measure of voluntary compliance and tests of it. As far as corporations doing business with the Government were concerned, the report called for contract compliance provisions to be established.
These recommendations in the Equality Now report were reflected in the Abella report in various ways, focusing on means by which equity in employment might be achieved. The judge has done a magnificent job in clarifying means in law and in institutions, in new provisions designed to smooth the way for a broader participation in employment among Canadians. These recommendations have had the support of various important bodies. The Canadian Ethno-Cultural Council and the Canadian Human Rights Commission have both recommended actions along these lines. I await the response of the Parliamentary Secretary.

speakeroldname: Mr. Geoff Scott (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: MULT1CULTURALISM-IMPLEMENTATION OF COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS. (B) ABELLA COMMISSION REPORT-DATE OF PRESENTATION
speechtext:
I wish to thank the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) for his observations and to assure him that this Government is committed to ensuring that there is equality of economic opportunity for all racial and cultural minority groups in our society.
I want to inform the Member that the Minister has submitted a number of recommendations to be included in the forthcoming government response to the Abella report Equality in Employment. As he may be aware, a number of those recommendations dealing with the employment sector have also been identified in Equality Now, the report of the special parliamentary committee on the participation of visible minorities in Canadian society. These dealt primarily with barriers which impede the full participation of visible minorities in the employment sector.
The results of a recent study in Toronto entitled Who gets the Work?, which was funded by the Multiculturalism Directorate, demonstrates that job barriers faced by visible minorities as a result of racial discrimination are major factors in the job search for individuals from these communities.
I want to say at this time that this Minister and this Government are strongly opposed to any form of racism and will direct the necessary energies to combat it with all the means at our disposal. Indeed, I can say that with the conviction of one who represents a riding in Hamilton with a
February 5, 1985

multiplicity of ethno-cultural groups unmatched anywhere in Canada.
Specifically, this Government will work co-operatively with the private sector to encourage the elimination of discriminatory practices in training and promotion. With respect to programs offered by Employment and Immigration Canada to the private sector, consideration will be given to the designation of visible minorities as a target group. In the public sector, the implementation of special measures for visible minorities will be introduced where necessary, following a survey of public service employees in the spring of 1985.
Of course, since any policy dealing with the elimination of discriminatory barriers involves more than just the federal Government, a strategy which includes provincial, municipal and other non-government agencies is being developed.
The Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Murta) has already started consultations with his provincial counterparts
Adjournment Debate
in order to have included in the forthcoming federal-provincial conference on multiculturalism a broad discussion dealing with the area of attitudinal and institutional change aimed at addressing a number of issues of major concern to Canada's cultural and racial minorities.
In conclusion, the Minister's multiculturalism officials have already developed a number of initiatives with the Federation of Canadian Municipalities and the Canadian Labour Congress to develop specific programs to overcome attitudes and practices that create limiting and unjust situations.
